utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]. You must stand up to introduce a new person who is next to you. Otherwise, we'll waste a lot of time if we make the introductions the same way. On behalf of the Bench I would like to greet all the people in the courtroom today. We must finish off with this hearing tomorrow and finish off the examination in chief and proceed with the cross-examination. Before giving the floor to Mr. Scott, as I told you yesterday, if you feel slightly tired or if you feel you need a rest, please let me know. If you cannot hold out for the entire morning, don't worry about it. Your testimony can be postponed until next Monday. So it's for you to decide. If you feel you are able to answer all the questions that will be put to you for the next four hours, that's fine. But if you feel you can't do this for health reasons, just let me know, and in that case we can postpone it until Monday. So how do things stand with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]. I will try and do my best. I will react if I'm feeling poorly, but I would prefer us to continue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we rely entirely on you. At any time, whenever you feel you would like to, you can stop the hearing. Mr. Scott, you said you needed 25 minutes. Could you make it even shorter than that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I will try, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pejanovic.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I think -- we went through a series of incidents or events yesterday afternoon, and I think there's only one additional event that we will cover this morning before proceeding on to some other items. Again with reference to your book, you mention that on the 2nd -- in the second half of January, 1994, there were fires at a number of locations including Velmos, Varteks and Opresa, and at the Marsal Tito Street. Can you just briefly tell the Chamber what you recall about those incidents, similar to what you did yesterday.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At all events, and it's quite true that that day we did have a series of very serious and strenuous interventions, it would be difficult to pinpoint one of them and say which was the most serious. Let me just enumerate -- well, not enumerate, but let me just say that at that point in time, the building was shelled or bombed of the former SDK, social accountancy service, which is where the command of the 4th Corps was put up at the time. And quite literally, a complete floor, a complete storey was destroyed and cut off. Then the next building underneath that section, below that section, I think it was in Marsala Tita Street, number 86, the fire broke out in apartment, and the building was built just a few years prior to the conflict. It was an attic and it was a very serious fire. We weren't able to apply any tactics for extinguishing fires. We had to go inside, which made it more difficult. But hand-in-hand with this we were targeted from Hum hill. And towards the evening there was another fire that broke out that I've already described in my book, and that was the fire that broke out on the so-called Varteks building. It takes its name from the fact that the Varteks company had a retail shop on the ground floor level, and everybody knew it as the Varteks building. Anyway, this fire broke out in an apartment there which was facing Hum hill. So quite literally if you were to look at it from Hum hill, you could see it with the naked eye, the building and the apartment, especially if you're using optic sights. Then of course you can see it even better, up close. Anyway, the apartment was set fire to with an inflammatory bullet, an incendiary bullet, and while we were there to put out the fire, there was a burst of gunfire sporadically from Hum, targeting the building in general terms, but visibility was poor for those shooting and also for us because we had to work in the dark and intervene in the dark. We weren't injured, luckily, but I think we stayed there and then withdrew. But there was somebody left on duty in the apartment next door, which faces north north-west. So it wasn't under threat at all. And there was a family living there, the Nova family, who knew us, and we stayed there all night, took shifts during the night, two shifts a night.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, when you -- what was your experience in terms of not only on this occasion but when you reported or responded to various fires or emergencies, did you find that the shelling or sniping stopped when the fire brigade arrived, or did it become more intense?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I really do have to say that when there was the general danger to all the citizens, that is to say when they all took refuge, we didn't have an alarm system, to begin with, to sound the general alarm, so when there was a general alarm, the only way people knew that it was an alarm was that you could hear the shelling and then people would rush and take shelter in the nearest shelter. So that was the time when we went out onto the streets, and that's when it was the greatest danger. But as luck would have it, and thank God we weren't hit when we went out. We didn't have any victims, casualties when with shelling went on. But it is true and it is a fact that on the buildings that we were extinguishing the fires, as soon as you could see that the fire was being put under control, the shooting would step up in intensity. For example, in Serif Buric Street, the fire that broke out there at the building that used to be the building of the former committee, party committee building, on the ground floor and in the basement of that building there was a hospital, a makeshift hospital, and I think that there was a communication system, but that's not the essential point now anyway. That floor was hit. And I couldn't understand for a long time how -- it appeared as if somebody was watching us while we were working, and as we managed to put the fires under control, the shooting would become more intensive, unscrupulous. And I thought about this and thought perhaps we were applying the wrong kind of tactics, because we -- I thought that they might have intercepted our communication lines when we were communicating with the fire brigade. Until at one point when I entered the street, because we entered it from Marsal Tito Street towards this Serif Buric Street, at that point when we entered the street while we were on our way, walking, going towards it, I saw projectiles being fired from Mrkan hill, and then I realised that they had their optic sights on us and could see us very well. And as they could see that the fire was diminishing and we were having it under control, the fire was a bit less intense, the intensity of the shelling increased. And another illustration of this, because one of the drivers failed to follow orders and in fact he was killed later on, one shell hit the concrete of a building and hit him in the head, and he was injured. It wasn't too serious. And another member was also hit by a grenade, a shell. There was a partition wall behind him, and that saved him from the shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So this explosion, the detonation that ensued, threw him, and he had injuries to his chest and he had to go on sick leave for 10 or 12 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Pejanovic, we need to move somewhat quickly this morning in order to try to stay on schedule, or do the best we can. Let me just ask you, please, before we continue, if you could mark on the map that we were using yesterday with the letter L the location of this incident that you've told us about this morning. In particular, at the Marshal Tito location. And for the record, we're again using or referring to the base map, which is Exhibit P09517.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but did you tell me to put the letter K there?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The letter L, please.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, just very briefly, please: You mentioned communications between yourself, the fire brigade, and perhaps other local authorities. Could you just briefly tell the Judges what the nature of your means of communication were during the second half of 1993 -- or from May, 1993, forward. Please focus your attention on that time period, May, 1993, forward, what the means of communication were.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number of radio stations that we had were insufficient. We had three transmitters, walkie-talkie devices, and in our vehicles -- in two vehicles we also had stationary stations, or mobile ones, whatever you like to call them, which were in the vehicles. All this was well and good and functioned properly when you have a proper system of communicating and when you have repeater stations and can reach your centre and communicate with it. However, in view of the short range of those devices and because of the configuration of the terrain that we acted in, we were not able to have communications coming over loud and clear, especially when you know that the left bank, since the beginning of the aggression, was completely cut off in terms of energy, water, electricity, that kind of thing, heating system, and so on. And the greatest problem we had in our fire brigade service was the lack of kilowatt hours for our repeater station and our stable base station to get power and then to tie ourselves in with the system. So that was a problem. But when we did have enough power, that was just symbolic. And in the department store named Razvitak, their generator stayed there and the generator would take over when the city network was down. So that was a fairly strong generator. It was made in that way for a certain number of kilowatt hours for the purposes of the department store. However, afterwards, we had a makeshift generator, and it had to deal with a lot, so we were allocated just a very small number of kilowatt hours, which meant that we could switch on our transistor radios to see the news in the evening. And it wasn't a continuous interval and signal, not 24 hours. But in the space of 24 hours, we were -- the generator was switched on for two or three hours, and if you managed to switch on at that particular time, you could hear something and listen through your own devices, but otherwise, everything was down. And their range was not that great either, due to the configuration of the terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, a final question on that point: When the radio system, for whatever reason, when your radios were not working, what was the means of communication? By example, if there was a fire in town in East Mostar and your radio system was not working, how would you at the fire brigade receive information about the fire?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 99 per cent - not to say 100 per cent - it went by word of mouth. That is to say, if somebody noticed a fire in the Tekija region, for example, would try and reach the unit by car, if they had one, or they would convey the messages, oral messages, and that would reach us. So what would happen is that sometimes more than half an hour elapsed and even an hour between the moment the fire broke out until the time we reached information about the fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. If I could have the witness please be shown Exhibit P04240. If we could have that displayed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you're able to see that document now --

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Of course I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- could you please tell us what that document is and what -- the information it provides.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a report, a piece of information required by the civilian protection service, and we were duty-bound to inform the civilian protection service about any serious interventions. In addition to that, we, of course, informed, sent out information on a monthly basis about fires, about the training and employees in the unit, any equipment that we needed, and things like that. So that was regular information sent out to the civilian protection staff and headquarters. This particular information says that from the 9th of May -- how many interventions there were from the 9th of May to the 16th of August, outside and inside, that is to say inside buildings and outside in the open air. We also note that the fires were usually caused by the fighting, by the shooting and the war, and that members of the unit were very often exposed to sniper fire or shelling and shrapnel during situations of that kind. And I have to add that I myself was a member of the staff dealing with protection measures for -- against fires both on land and at sea, on the water, and so I sent out information to the civilian protection staff and headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we can proceed next, Mr. Pejanovic, and in final couple -- series of questions, I would like to show you -- in the interests of time --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, in the interests of time, what I've done is provide the next bundle of exhibits, which I'll give to you in a moment, in one single combined bundle in the B/C/S versions to hand to the witness so we can proceed as quickly as possible. If I could have the assistance of the usher, please. And while she's doing this, I'll indicate in the record what's being given to the witness. Your Honours and for the Defence, the bundle of material that's been put before the witness now is Exhibit P07996.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, Mr. Pejanovic, while I'm reading these numbers, if you can look at that bundle that's been put in front of you and just generally see what it is so I can briefly ask you a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I just have to take a look at the first page, I don't need the rest, just to see who my colleagues were. This is once again a report going to the civilian protection staff, and in keeping with what I said a moment ago, we were duty-bound to send out regular reports and information to the staff about any problems that might have cropped up during our work. And since the civilian protection staff, pursuant to an order of the republican civilian protection staff, probably had to collect data about fatalities and casualties, then the civilian protection staff under extraordinary circumstances would send in a request or a piece of information according to which it would say that said they needed the data on so-and-so. So this information must be provide -- might have been provided pursuant to a special request from the civilian protection staff or a regular request. And as I said, we did send out regular reports to the civilian protection, because we who were heads of sectors, heads of departments, were duty-bound to have meetings every fortnight to analyse the situation in our departments.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, Mr. Pejanovic, I'm not going to take you again, partly for the interests of time and partly because the information is shown on the face of the document, I'm not going to take you through these one by one in detail, and I'm not going to mention --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In order to avoid going into private session, Mr. President, I'm not going to ask the witness to mention any of these names which again are on the face of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness, just as a general matter, if I can direct your attention, as one example only, to Exhibit P07996, which should be the first item in your bundle. If you could just focus on that for a moment. Is it correct, sir, that basically each of these reports is a report concerning either a wounded or killed firefighter, and the form will give the person's name, date of birth, various other information, and the date and nature of the either injury or death? Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, without a doubt, because we received this form. We didn't compile it, we received it from the Ministry of Defence, and then they would send it on. And I think this is a standard form, the standard form that was used for reports and information of this nature. So it's a standard form. It's not one that we compiled. We just received a questionnaire from the civilian protection authorities, and then we had to fill in this form entering all the data, even the mother's name and her maiden name. So that this was the standard type of form, and we couldn't change it or influence it in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And all these forms that I've just handed to you and listed for the record, these were all forms and records that were made and completed by the fire-fighting unit in the course of its duties in 1993, 1994; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, undoubtedly so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Pejanovic, I thank you on behalf of the Prosecution for your testimony and assistance to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, that completes the Prosecution examination. We would tender at this time into evidence the following documents: P04240, P07996, P07997, P07998, P07999, P08001, P08003, P08005, P08007, P08009, P09139, P09140, P09220, P09511, P09512, P09513, and P09517, both in its form as the original base map, if you will; that's the map -- that is the base map that the witness has been using the last two days, and I would ask for an in-court exhibit number to be provided to the marked map that the witness has marked, that that will be given a number as a new exhibit. And, Your Honour, concerning the bundle of records that we've given to the witness this morning, I would ask that those at least momentarily be kept under seal because of the names and information that's reflected in the documents. It may be that what can be done in the future is that a redacted version can be provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You have -- on your list of documents we have P9139, and there's a blank here. Oh, it's a video. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: P9139 is the 360-degree video, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's a video, then. Registrar, you will have to retrieve the marked map, and that marked map will have to have a specific number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. This map -- in English, this map will have a number IC0002. [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] on the P9517. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, as far as the others are concerned -- yes, Mr. Scott, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It was just to complete the thought. In terms of the bundle of records that were provided to the witness just a few minutes ago, I would propose, Your Honour, and we'd ask that those be initially kept under seal because of the names and information that are reflected on the face of the documents of some of the victims. I would anticipate that what might be done in the future is certain items could be redacted and then the document, once redacted, then can be otherwise public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So to begin with and to gain time, Registrar, we shall accept the numbers of documents which have been quoted: 4240, 7996, 7997, 7998, 7999, to 8001, 8003, 8005, 8007, 8009, 9539, which is a video, 9140, 9220, 9511, 9512, 9513 and 9517, which was the original document. We shall now move on to the cross-examination. The Chamber -- the Bench has not ruled on the issue of disclosure of documents before the cross-examination. We shall rule on this next week. And at the end of this hearing, we shall discuss this. I assume that the Defence has not disclosed any documents, so we shall proceed as we did with the former witness. I shall now give the floor to Mr. Karnavas, who is the first to speak, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: My name is Michael Karnavas, and along with my colleagues, I represent Dr. Jadranko Prlic. I will ask you some very direct questions, and if we are able to get through them, hopefully we will have you back in Mostar for the weekend. So I would appreciate -- I will try to discipline myself in asking precise questions, and I trust you will provide me with direct answers. And if you need to make any explanations, please feel free. First, if I could talk to you a little bit about your background. I don't believe we heard about your educational background. What is it, sir?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're interested in the type of school that I concluded, I don't wish to discuss this. I'm ready to discuss what I wrote about, and this is the reason why I came here. Sir, I had a completely normal traditional training for firefighters. I was first a trainee firefighter, and then I went up the hierarchy to the top position. I even trained other firefighters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Would it be fair for us to assume, then, that your entire career has been in fire-fighting?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Out of 41 years and six months of my service years, I spent 21 years working as a professional firefighter, and prior to that I worked as a volunteer firefighter. And you can find all this information in the book that I wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sure it's in the book. I'm just trying to figure out what your training is and what your background is. I assume you did your JNA training, your military service training.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally. Naturally, yes. And I'm proud of having served in the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That was the same army, incidentally, that you referred to in your statement as the Chetniks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't place them in the same category. I'm proud of having served in the army in 1963 to 1965. The other army, this other armada attacking the town and Bosnia-Herzegovina, none of us should discuss it. We should leave it to the historians, because we're not competent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But nonetheless, that was the army, the other armada that you called Chetniks, which I understand is sort of a pejorative term that often is used to describe Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used that term consciously, because I differentiate between an honest and decent Serb and a Chetnik on the other hand. That is a great difference there. Anybody who is prepared to commit a crime has a name, and that name can either be Chetnik, Ustasha, or Ballista. And decent, honest Serbs are something quite different. I consider myself to be one of them because I remained in my town where for thousands of years my ancestors lived and worked, and I'm very proud of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: As you should be, sir. But as I -- if I understand you correctly yesterday, some of your neighbours perhaps thought that you were one of the Chetniks, too, when they were asking you why you're going around with that walkie-talkie, or did I misunderstand that incident which you considered a -- to be a provocation?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you misunderstood it. That incident took place in the street where I live, and I described it, saying that I took the walkie-talkie because at the time we still had a relatively normal supply of electricity, so that the central station in our headquarters operated normally. It was more likely to lose telephone connection so that I would lose contact with my colleagues, and this is why I asked to take walkie-talkie with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not questioning your intentions. What I am suggesting, however, from your answers yesterday, your neighbours were alluding to the fact that perhaps, you having the walkie-talkie, you were one of them. Is that how you took it at the time when they asked you, "Why are you carrying this walkie-talkie? Who are you talking to?"

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat: I think that you are stating this arbitrarily. These were my fellow citizens, my fellow Serbs. They were asking me why I had a walkie-talkie because they were fearing that perhaps I was in the service of some other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Exactly. The Chetnik side.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would they think that I was a Chetnik if I was amongst my own? Why would they believe that? Had I been among the Chetniks, then they would have known that that's what I am. What happened there is that there could have been fears that I was an Ustasha or a Ballista, because I was among my own people, and there is no way they would have thought that I was a Chetnik because that would imply that they were Chetniks too. No. It could have only meant that I crossed over to the opposite side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you also considered it a provocation when they asked you to bring out your weapons, I guess the assumption being, you being a Serb, obviously you would have weapons in your house, which was in fact not the case.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is likely that that's what they thought, but they were wrong. I had absolutely no weapons on me. And let me just give you an illustration: The kind of job I performed required me to carry a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, if I may intervene. I don't need lengthy explanations. I just want -- if you can answer the questions directly, I might be able to get you home today or tomorrow. So the answer is they assumed - and I'm underscoring the word "assumed" - because you were a Serb, obviously you would have in your home weapons, and that's why you took an affront to that, because it was an assumption; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I confirm that clearly. I assume so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that's why they asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah. And you felt offended.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I was offended, but I didn't feel good about them asking me this, because I thought that they knew very well who had weapons and who didn't. I didn't have that information, but I'm sure that they knew that very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And as a result of that question being posed to you, you stopped going out at night along with your neighbours and just continued on with your own work, which dealt with civil protection matters; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After that night, I stopped being on duty in the street, not stopped communicating with my neighbours. I stopped being on duty, and I started spending 24 hours with other firefighters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we're going to speak a little bit about your fire-fighting career and your activities with the civil protection, but first I would like to touch upon the topic that was last discussed by the Prosecution. Perhaps I could begin by asking you whether you are -- you have any special military training with respect to ballistics.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And artillery?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And I said so yesterday in my evidence that I was not a strategic expert nor a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it you're not hunter either. Since you didn't have any weapons at home, you're probably not a hunter.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So I take it if I were to go --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The mike is on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So I take it if we were to go into a lengthy discussion with respect to trying to figure out the angles of the wounds and where the shots would have come to in order to locate the so-called snipers, perhaps you're not the best person to get into this discussion with; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never claimed so. However, I think it's right for me to speak about what I saw, and that's what I spoke about. I never claimed anything about the direction of trajectory nor anything about ballistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And while you were able -- I noticed in the film you were saying, "It was from there," when you were directing, and you were pointing this way and that way - and the record should reflect that I'm gesturing, you know, with my hands - other than that, that's the best you can do to tell us where the shots were coming from; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a suggestion, if the Trial Chamber will agree with me. Sir, why don't you come to Mostar, and I will take you to this location where the water truck was and where they were shooting from. I have no better way of explaining this to you. This was not secondhand information, no; I was an eyewitness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And after the -- the one incident that you described yesterday, as I understand it, you didn't see the individual get hit. You heard about it, and then you saw the person on the ground; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you be more explicit? Which incident do you have in mind? When I was pointing with my hands yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No. Yesterday, when you were describing where your colleague was shot, and he survived for a day and then the following day he passed away. Now, on that particular incident --

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uzeir. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah. You didn't see the sniper.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody ever saw a single sniper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to go step-by-step. You weren't watching -- you weren't watching your colleague at the moment that he was shot.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I heard him as he said, "Oh, mother," and when he dropped to his knees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And when you turned to see him, he was -- was he on the ground or was he still standing up? Was he standing up?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I said to you, and as I said very clearly, he was on his left knee and his left elbow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So you don't know and you cannot tell us with any degree of precision in which direction he was facing at the time that he was shot.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I claim this emphatically. I know this. He was turned with his back toward the bullet that hit him. Otherwise, he could not have been hit under his left shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That, I think, we can figure out. What I'm asking is with precision on the ground where exactly he was and how he was turned and where the sniper was coming from. You cannot tell us with any degree of precision, can you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you this very precisely. He had his back turned. I was on his right. The bullet came from his -- from the direction to where his back was turned to, and the bullet entered under his left shoulder. And I never attempted to do anything about the sniper because it was other snipers hunting snipers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand, sir, nor am I suggesting that you should have done something. I'm just trying to get some basic information. And you answered my next question, which was: After that incident you did not do any investigation nor did anyone else do any investigation to try to find out the exact location of the sniper.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, sir, you're forgetting that this was immediately after the war. No investigations were conducted even in much more serious cases. And if we analyse those who should have initiated an investigation, I was the last person down in that chain. What was to be expected of me was to give information, provide a report, go and visit his family, and do what was humane. It was up to others to conduct an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So the answer to my question is no; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did no investigation, nor did anybody else to my knowledge, but I'm pointing this out for the record that during those days many other incidents were not investigated either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, yesterday you indicated and you brought our attention to the potential sniper being at a particular building. It was a bank building. The Privredna bank building. I'm a little tongue-tied today. That's the name of the building; right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And on -- if we go back to yesterday's transcript, on page 108, on lines 5 to 6, you said the opposite side tried to hit that sniper to put him out of action. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And when you were referring to the other side, is it not a fact that you were referring to the HVO? Correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that the HVO would be trying to hit their own sniper. It would be more natural for the members of the army to try to hit the enemy sniper, because they were enemies of each other. So why would somebody look for their own sniper?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Are you aware of a mixed group of HVO and ABiH who tried to locate that sniper at that particular building? Are you aware of any of that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's the first I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. You're not suggesting that it never occurred?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say either way. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And assuming that that is the case, that there was a mixed group of HVO along with the ABiH who tried to locate, isolate, and take out that particular sniper, then I take it that my earlier question, the opposite side would also include the HVO trying to take out that particular sniper?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour, to both the form of the question and it assumes facts not in evidence. Why should this witness simply answer questions based on Mr. Karnavas's pure assumptions. I object to that, and I object also to the complexity of the question. It's not clear at this point what's being asked, who is on what side. The witness gave a very clear answer previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I -- very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I intended to ask the witness a question about this. As Mr. Karnavas mentioned a few moments ago, the witness did say in his testimony yesterday that people had tried to shoot this sniper, and page 20, line 15, this morning, he also said that other snipers were hunting this sniper. So in the interests of justice, it is important to understand who was shooting at this sniper. So quite rightly so, we should ask the witness who were these people shooting at the sniper? Did they belong to the mixed group? Were they unidentified people? Who were these people? I think this is a relevant question. Mr. Karnavas, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, if indeed there was a mixed group of HVO and ABiH -- and I have a good faith basis for asking the question, Mr. Scott very well knows that. If Mr. Scott is not aware of his own evidence, then I'll move on, Your Honour. Today, the first incident that was mentioned by Mr. Scott in that particular building, do you recall talking about it this morning, the first incident? The former social accounting service building, I believe it is.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but this did not involve a sniper. It involved artillery shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting that it was. I'm going to bring you back. We're going to go in and out of various areas. In that particular building, is it not a fact that there was one military unit of the ABiH in that particular building? And I believe you even mentioned it in your book on page 56, as I'm sure Mr. Scott is aware of.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's no secret. All prisoners of the HVO, all those who were imprisoned, know that for a while in the basement of that building there was a prison. For a while. I stress for a while. And then there was a command headquarters as well. So that's no secret. You also have to know that two or three prisoners escaped. So all of that enabled the information to be passed on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, when you say it was -- it was a command post, we're talking about the command of the -- of the 4th Corps, right, of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So that's a military target, is it not? Or maybe, because of your background, you wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I have to warn you that you are being ironic, and I'd like to ask you to refrain from that. We're in the courtroom. So I kindly ask you not to do that. Yes, I'm aware of that, that that's a military target, but I'm also telling you that the building number 86, next to it, was a civilian location; the building across from it, Varteks, the same. Building number 96, too, was a civilian facility, so you can't keep telling me that all of those were military targets. This one, this particular one, yes, it was a military target.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that. Yesterday, you indicated that there was sniping on both sides; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably, I believe so. I believe that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You believe or it was indeed a fact? And I'm not being ironic on this one. Okay? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. And I'm not being ironic either. As that was the case yesterday, in the course of my testimony I said that a colleague of mine from the other side who was put up with us was hit by a sniper in the Bulevar, the location of the former clinic, and that means that there was a sniper who opened fire from the other side. It's not moral, but is it unnatural to return fire? That's why there was a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. In fact, there was -- let's face it, this was urban combat fighting, was it not? Both sides shooting at each other.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. That's evident. But the army, the armija, had nowhere near the amount of materiel and equipment. It had nowhere near the amount of materiel and equipment that the HVO had. I'm not here to judge anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And neither are we, but I'm trying to get to the facts. Would you -- would it -- can we assume that since there was sniping from the east to the west, that the commander of the 4th Corps, Mr. Pasalic, was the one that had ordered that sniping? Can we make that assumption?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm again going to object to that question, Your Honour. Again based on facts not in evidence. Pure assumption, pure speculation on behalf of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. The whole point is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. As to this objection, because you are now in the realm of absolute speculation, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And the point being that yesterday the gentleman was making assumptions all day long and I'm trying to bring the point home. What's good for the direct is good for the cross. If he's going to assume all sorts of things that the HVO was doing, I'm trying to get to this from the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You can't make that assumption, can you, sir, that these were ordered snipers?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour. Nothing's changed. It's pure speculation for this witness, pure assumption, and cannot assist the Chamber in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, Mr. Scott, but within the scope of cross-examination, the Defence counsel are entitled to provide their interpretation, asking for the witness to give his point of view. Anyway, this will be judged and assessed by the Judges. This doesn't harm anybody, because if it is pure speculation, unfounded, not relying on documents, it doesn't have any probative value. Please, Mr. Karnavas, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can we assume that Mr. Pasalic perhaps was acting on the orders of Alija Izetbegovic, his commander-in-chief, and that he had effective command and control over all the sniping that was going on from the east to the west? Can we make that assumption simply because sniping was occurring?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think you're asking the wrong person if you're asking you me about this. You should ask the late Alija Izetbegovic and Mr. Arif Pasalic. They're both deceased. I don't know whether this is something that is stated somewhere in the transcript but I am really not interested in this. I was discussing the matter of firefighters, and I was telling you about the events that we experienced in the course of 1991 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, yesterday you indicated about an incident where you thought -- or you were told that perhaps a Chinese missile was used, something to that effect. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I remember that. It was about Blagaj and about targeting Tekija at the top of Blagaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Tekija, that incident is not in your book, is it? I couldn't find it.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you're right. I didn't describe this in my book. When -- I said something about this in the course of an interview, an oral statement I made in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, when -- I thought from yesterday that this was -- the first time you mentioned this to the Prosecution was two days ago when you arrived. Are you suggesting now that you gave a statement in Mostar to the investigators here about this particular incident?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had interviews on five occasions in Mostar, and perhaps that statement was given in an unofficial way. Perhaps it wasn't an official interview, because a lot of time has passed since then so it's not possible for me to remember all the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Nonetheless, when you mentioned that there was this Chinese missile, that was based on information that you had received, not information that you had observed; right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but in fact you are partially right, because I heard about this from a colleague who was in Blagaj. He was the commander of that department. I heard that it was a Chinese mortar. This wasn't the first time Blagaj had been shelled in this manner, so he probably had such experience. I know that there were three missiles that were launched one after another, and they passed over our heads and fell somewhere up in the hills. Well, a rough estimate would be 2 or 300 metres away, or a hundred metres to the left from the -- from the top of that location, from the top of -- from the top of the Buna bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Other than being told that this was a Chinese missile, you have nothing else to verify that; right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't interested in that, to tell you the truth. All I was interested in was fleeing from that location where I heard the screeching of the missile. I'd like to see how you would behave in such a situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, I don't mean to be impolite and I don't want to disrupt you or interrupt you, but the question was: Other than being told, you have no other information. Now, that calls for a yes or no answer. Could you cooperate with us.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've answered your question. I said no, apart from what I heard from my colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you don't know whether your colleague was correct or incorrect.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume he was correct, because prior to that event there was another incident. Three multiple rocket launchers were fired, three missiles hit the fishpond, and the mother of the Zutina family was killed, because they lived opposite the fishpond. So pieces of the missile remained there, and that's probably how they assessed the situation. As I have said, I wasn't really interested in everything. At the time, all I wanted to do was to flee from the site of the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Getting back to the substance, are you not simply, sir, assuming that your friend was correct when he said that this was a Chinese missile? And I guess that's the point that I'm trying to get at; that you're making all of these assumptions.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not an assumption. I'm claiming that this happened. I'm claiming that three missiles flew over our heads and fell somewhere in the hills. I am making an assumption when --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Chinese missile. That's what the question was. Are you not, sir, making an assumption that this was a Chinese missile and that your friend was correct? That's the question. If you don't understand it, I'll rephrase it, but we can move along if you just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not necessary to do that. You said quite clearly that I was assuming that it was a Chinese missile and I assume that I had seen it. I am not assuming that I saw it, but I am assuming that it was a Chinese missile, and that assumption is based on what my colleague told me. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, just one point before we move on: The demarcation line was not the river itself; right? That's not what separated the two conflicting parties.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to say where the line was. It's true that in part of the town it was the river that represented the demarcation line. In the other part of the town, there was the river and the Hum hill that in fact represented the line of demarcation. And then in the third part of town there was a street which was the demarcation line. There were MUP members on one side and HVO members on the other side. Then this Santica Street, the other part of Santica Street from the Partizan Kino and further up, and that street also represented the demarcation line. But when I mentioned the demarcation line and said that the distances were not very significant, what I wanted to say was that it was very difficult to say where the front lines started and where they stopped, because in the eastern part of town, well, the area's very small, and there were the Serbian forces on the one side and the Croatian forces on the other side. So it's very difficult to state where the demarcation line was exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But in town itself, you mentioned one street. The Bulevar is the other; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said up to Hum, there was the Bulevar. From Spanish Square right up to the Hum hill. And the Bulevar represented the demarcation line there. The HVO was on Hum, and down below there was the ABiH. But from Santica Street towards the Bulevar -- or, rather, from the former Mose Pijade Street there's the Spanca Street, which was divided, and from that part towards Carinski bridge, the street also represented the demarcation line. So it's very difficult to understand all of this unless you actually visit the site and see what it looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Perhaps you can help us out here by just referring to the map that was used by the Prosecution. I believe it was given a new name, IC0002. Previously it was P09517. If we could --

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gladly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good. We're moving along. If I could get some assistance and just put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, if it will save time this morning, I don't think there's any dispute by anyone in the courtroom --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm entitled to do my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- we can agree that the area marked in yellow on the map and described as the Bulevar, and then you can see Santica Street, that that was generally the demarcation line. The Prosecution does not dispute that; we can agree that that's the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm thankful for that observation. First of all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One minute, Mr. Karnavas, as to the objection raised by the Prosecution. I think it's important for the witness to tell us where the ABiH was, where the HVO was, and listening to him I realise that there was also -- that there were Serbian forces. So it might be interesting, based on this map, for this -- these forces to be positioned even if he's not a military expert, I mean, in spite of the fact that he served for two years in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... witness to tell us as opposed to the Prosecutor testifying for us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I'll write down "HVO" for the part that was covered by the HVO, and I'll use the letter A to mark the area covered by the army or armija. [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you could just help us out here. I know you marked it, but just show us --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Karnavas, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you could just show us, sir, on the map.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we turn this around and approach it from the south? Let's have a look at the place where it says Donja Mahala. In fact, let's start from the south. You can see that it says Donja Mahala here, and I've marked this with the letter A. This is the Dzemal Bijedic road and ends at the Hasan Brkic bridge. You have a green line here. There is an HVO sign here. This is the part towards Cekrek and towards Hum. If we continue northwards down the Bulevar as far as the Spanish Square, the Spanski Trg, we're talking about the left side now if you're looking from the north to the south. On left side of the Bulevar, this area was covered by the armija. I've marked this. On the right side you have an area covered by the HVO. This has also been marked, with the letters "HVO." Around this street Onesuk Street, there's part -- there's part that is near Hum, but I couldn't really say how -- what the distance is here. But this part was also under the armija, and this part was blown up, because a good -- the friend of a good -- the son of a good friend of mine was killed as a result of a mine. If you head off -- if you set off from the Spanski Trg down Mose Pijade Street and turn into the first street on the right, here it says the HVO, and then in the lower part you also have an area where it says Kolvarska, and I've marked this with "HVO." This area is also under the HVO. Here it says A, and then there is a cul-de-sac that is in the direction of the Neretva River. It's only three metres wide, this street. Half was under the armija and the other half under the HVO. This part ends with the street that leads from the Carinski bridge to Hotel Ero, or the pensioners hotel, and that is what the balance of power in the town was. Those are the positions. As far as the Serbs are concerned, it's impossible to mark their positions on the map here because, from this line here that you can now see, if you have a look at this extreme point here, where it says "Bjelusine," well, from there to the demarcation line with the Serbs, the distance was between three or four kilometres as the crow flies. Perhaps I've overestimated the distance, but that would be my estimate because those positions were mostly in part of Podvelezje and the armija was in that area, which was divided; you had the armija on one side and the Serbs on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I take it we don't quite see it on the map, but these are narrow streets and tight corners where this urban combat was going on; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that this was street combat. People would just open fire on positions, provoke each other. I'm not a strategical expert but I was a lay juror and I assisted -- I was present to war crimes trials in the area that I live in. And one of the issues was why was it necessary to exert such pressure in the town? And the answer was in order to relief the pressure on forces in Bijelo Polje or -- or the reverse; in order to ensure that the demarcation line in the town was relieved in a certain sense. I'm not being ironical. It was necessary to be -- to live through such conditions to know how terrible this shelling was and how terrible it was when snipers started -- started firing at random.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Thank you very much, sir. Now, I want to go back in time, actually, and since you mentioned the Serbs, I assume that you are referring to the JNA and -- and also the reservists that had come from Montenegro when you were referring to their position. So I want to talk about that period. Okay?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I'm concerned, that's fine. I don't know whether it's directly related to this trial, but I won't avoid discussing the matter and I'll tell you whatever I know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. In early -- early April, 1992, Mostar was attacked, was it not?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of April, on the 3rd of April, to be precise, 1993, the barracks of the Mostar Battalion was blown up. There were reservists billeted in those barracks, and part of the armed forces of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And we're talking about the JNA; correct? That's what they called themselves. Others called them Chetniks. But we're talking about the JNA or what remained of the JNA, along with reservists from Montenegro; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to discuss that. I clearly defined the term "Chetnik" and the term "Serbian." And please don't try to engage me in such discussions again, because I think that this amounts to offending innocent Serbs. In the territory of the federation, 180.000 Serbs remained who were loyal to Bosnia and Herzegovina. They weren't all Chetniks if they had weapons that were from Bosnia and Herzegovina, that were part of Bosnia and Herzegovina or the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not trying to offend you. I'm merely making the point then that this is the JNA that others referred to as the Chetniks. Isn't that correct? We're talking about the JNA forces. The same forces that had attacked Croatia, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, let me repeat this: I distinguish between the JNA and the Chetniks. When the reservists entered Mostar, that's when Chetniks might have appeared. Scum might have appeared. Chetnik scum might have appeared at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And at some point a Crisis Staff was formed, was it not?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we're talking for the municipality of Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that was sort of normal, because that's what the law provided for. In case of emergencies, a Crisis Staff would be formed. So it wasn't an abnormal activity.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- these were legal activities, legal authorities. It was a legal army that was the only legal representative or the only legal force defending Yugoslavia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I want to focus now on -- on the Mostar municipality. There was an attempt to mobilise, was there not, within the municipality to counter this attack? Correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the municipality of Mostar, but general mobilisation had been declared. The former JNA had declared general mobilisation, but many quite simply didn't respond to this general mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Especially in Mostar, as you so rightly told us, that out of 13 units, only two responded with respect to the fire-fighting units; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please be a little patient, I'll try to explain this to you. Those 13 units were part of the fire brigade association, but they had different structures. That means that within the organisation, there were fire-fighting units that belonged to companies, there were volunteer fire-fighting units within companies, there were territorial and professional fire-fighting units. There were 13 such units at the beginning of the conflict. None of the territorial fire-fighting units, since there were only two, one was a volunteer unit and the other was professional, they stayed on. There was the professional fire company, and all the volunteer units ceased functioning. All the company fire-fighting units ceased functioning because it was war time, so they automatically ceased functioning. That would be my explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I believe you mentioned that yesterday, and you mentioned in your book that out of 13 units, only two reported to duty?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. You have to bear in mind that there were two joint detachments, and there were fire-fighting units and neither of them responded. We combined members from that organisation and from the Mostar fire-fighting association, and we formed a wartime fire-fighting unit by combining these forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that nothing much was functioning in the municipality as a result of -- of the war activities? At the early stages, I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it didn't really function later on either. You're quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we have been working for an hour and a half. We're going to have a 15-minute break, and we shall resume at quarter to eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before the -- before the break, we left off -- we had gone back in time to 1992, April, to be precise, when the reservists, along with the JNA or the Serb forces, had attacked Mostar, and we'd indicated that a Crisis Staff had been formed, and in fact it was Mr. Gagro who was appointed as the president of the Crisis Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the formation of a Crisis Staff, as we indicated, was not something out of the usual, it was built into the law for cases of emergency, and this indeed - this occasion - was such an emergency; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, as I -- as I understand it, it was around April 9th or April 10th when the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina had declared an imminent threat of war in Mostar municipality. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that. I knew that that was done, but I can't tell you the exact date now. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in that decision, it had specifically requested the Yugoslav People's Army, those units that were in Bosnia-Herzegovina, to -- to leave; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, to withdraw.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The decision indicated that Mostar municipality was partially occupied by the Yugoslav People's Army; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Along with paramilitary forces. And that they were carrying out -- that is, the Yugoslav People's Army and paramilitary forces were carrying out armed attacks on civilians; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. The only question is where were they civilians and where were they organised armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Correct. And there was looting of businesses and family houses?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to appeal to the Trial Chamber for us not to go into all that, and I'll tell you why: My book encompasses the period of 1992 as much as was necessary for our activities and operations. I don't wish to answer questions of this kind, because they are designed to provoke me. I am not a strategic expert, and least of all do I wish to discuss what happened, because if I were to say that the Serbs withdrew and that they -- the apartments were left full of all kinds of property and things, you won't believe me. So I don't want to enter into those waters at all, and I'd like to ask you to stop asking me questions of that nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, I didn't intervene so far, but I have realised that all the questions you have put since the beginning are questions which you can put to the expert witness who will be testifying on Monday. He is an expert on -- on fires and troubleshooting, but not in geostrategy matters. So if you ask him a question about things which we don't know about, and the book is not being presented as evidence, perhaps he has tackled political issues we are not aware of in his book, but we, the Bench will have to render a judgement on the basis of things which are discussed here, on the basis of things which are presented in an indictment and presented in statements on fundamental issues, paragraphs 111 of the pre-trial brief. You are now wasting time on issues which can be addressed next week. The witness does not wish to answer the question. Don't belabour the point, please. Have you understood me? On several occasions he has said he did not wish to answer, and you are obliging him to answer questions for which -- which he is not -- which he cannot answer. You can put him questions or ask him questions about fire-fighting and other issues, but these other questions, ancillary questions, I'm not so interested in. These experts that will be testifying at a later stage can answer those questions. So set these questions aside and put them to more competent or qualified witnesses. You are in the presence of a witness who does not wish to answer these questions for personal reasons and which are perfectly understandable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, with all due respect, what I was reading was a preamble from a decision of the Municipal Crisis Staff of Mostar, so I wasn't trying to engage the gentleman in a political discussion but, rather, setting up the stage and its background information. But very well, I take the point. But I should also add if the gentleman does not wish to answer certain questions, then I would be asking that his testimony be stricken from the evidence, his direct. The Prosecution cannot bring witnesses here that will only answer the Prosecution's questions, even when they are outside the indictment, and then when its the Defence asking the questions, they choose not to ask [sic]. But very well, Your Honour. I take the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, based on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, this is not what I have said. You have just told us that you have a document pertaining to the Mostar Crisis Staff. Then show him the document and ask him to comment on this. You are putting questions on a document which we do not have and we don't know what this document is all about. So if we apply the procedure the way it should be, you should show him the document and then ask him questions about it. I don't think that this document that concerns the Crisis Staff, I don't think this document will talk about the declaration of war. But if you want to pursue with this line of questions, in that case, please show the witness this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. And again I don't mean to be disrespectful, I'm just trying to save some time. If I get a yes to the question, I don't need to show the document. I'm trying to save some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In any event, at some point in April 29th was there not a decision, sir, if you recall, was there not a decision that was made by the Crisis Staff for the HVO Mostar Municipal Staff and members of the Ministry of Interior of the Mostar centre to be in charge for the protection and defence of the city of Mostar? Were you aware of that? April 29th.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat: I was not aware of that, but I'll say what I said yesterday, that on the 30th of June that Crisis Staff and legally elected government at the 1990 election was toppled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Were you aware, sir, of this decision, April 29, 1992, where the Crisis Staff itself appoints the HVO Mostar Municipal Staff and members of the Ministry of Interior of the Mostar centre to be in charge for the protection and defence of the city? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I was not aware of that, so I repeat: I don't know about that. But you have a document that was published in the book with all the dates, and when Mr. Roko Markovina was still the commander of the civilian protection staff, Civil Defence Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Are you aware that on May 15, 1992, the HVO Mostar Municipal Staff issued an order based on the decision in principle of April 29th, since they were in charge of -- of -- of the defence of the city of Mostar, that an order was issued to disband the Crisis Staff? Were you aware of that? This is May 15, 1992.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I repeat that. Because I had an order of the 18th -- or, rather, the 22nd of April, 1992, signed by Mr. Roko Markovina, and it was published in the book, as I say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, let me make sure we're on the same wavelength. This is May 15. The HVO Mostar Municipal Staff issued an order to disband the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Mostar and gave to the special purpose council of the Mostar Municipal Staff of the HVO the obligations to administer the entire functioning of the city. Are you aware of that? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've repeated this twice, sir: No. But I have an order which is dated the 22nd of April. And let me repeat once again that all the shifts in town were organised in July, that is to say after June, 1992, and I say that with full responsibility. Now, when the decisions were actually made, I really can't say. And just take a look at the order, for instance, of the civilian defence staff in Visoko and the date, and that will be quite clear to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sometime in the middle of June Mostar was liberated; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Between the 12th and 14th of June, that's when the operation took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It was the HVO that liberated Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't agree with you fully there because the HVO did not act on its own. Quite literally, and without wishing to insult anybody who was a member of the BH army or MUP, but together with the HVO you had the BH army taking part together and the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina as legal creations and entities of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Are you suggesting that the army of BiH existed on the -- on the east side in May and in June and that they were the ones that were liberating that part of the town? Is that your suggestion, sir?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, let me repeat for the umpteenth time. You're trying to be very provocative. Shame on you because of that. And I'm going to repeat this: I said quite clearly that within the composition of the HVO forces you had the forces of the Mostar Battalion as a component part of the BH army, not on the left side of town but they were together with the HVO members on the right bank and were put up in Vranica, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is to say they acted together; the BH army, the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as the legal forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, acted in cohort.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The east side, sir, is it not fact, had fallen at some point, and folks such as yourself had to evacuate and go to the west side?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. On the 13th of May, the entire left bank was taken over by Serb forces, and I left on the 11th of May with a group of members and a vehicle that remained in working order. The other vehicle was already in the western part of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And -- and that's the side, by the way, where you would expect the Muslim forces to be fighting against the Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that that's what they did, because they acted together with the HVO forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the terrain is not very friendly for those who are living on the east side, and I'm speaking about the events when the Serbs were attacking, because the Serbs had the high ground; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A little later the ratio and relationship changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But what I'm suggesting is - correct me if I'm wrong - that when the Serbs - and I'm talking about the aggressors - were attacking Mostar, and in particular the east side, they had the high ground with the residents of the east bank more or less being like fish in a barrel where they could be picked off and shot at.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In neither part were the citizens spared. They were equally exposed to that Golgotha of being picked off by snipers, the effects of shrapnel, and anything else that was used to shoot at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Of course the difference being that these fled to the west, and not vice versa.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But then they fled or, rather, returned from the west or were expelled from where they were residing and reached the same position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I take it - and correct me if I'm wrong - that during -- during that period, the city, both on the east and on the west, was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you by any chance document the exact destruction caused by the Serbs on the east side?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Truth to tell, that does exist somewhere in the reports and information, and I might have mentioned that. I'm not ashamed of that. I wasn't involved. The people who perpetrated it should be ashamed. So I had no reason to cover that up. I just wrote my observations and assessed the situation and I think I did it very properly in my book, and I speak about the relationships and ratio of forces and that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And just to make sure that I have it right and that we're clear here, it was May 11, 1992, that the east side fell.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was the 13th of May, 1992, and I left on the 11th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I have it wrong then. So it fell on the 13th of May, and then we have that order that I referenced to on May 15th, two days later, which you're not aware of.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why should I be aware of it? Because I always had certain orders issued by the civilian protection staff, and they were parameters for my own work. Dear sir, it was easiest for me to collect up all the equipment, hand it over to the Serbs and perhaps move out with them. What could anybody do to me today? I wouldn't have been a war criminal, I would have been one of the thousands of people who left and returned. I didn't do that. I took the equipment that was accessible and the men that were accessible with me, and I thanked them for listening to me and we went together. There was one Serb among them and two Bosniaks. So thank you to those men for listening to me and going with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah. And I'm not being judgemental, sir. I'm merely trying to establish under whose order or under whose authority were you functioning? Because if you have a Crisis Staff --

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
