utterances.text: Mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we have an order of the May -- of May 15th disbanding the Crisis Staff, would it not stand to reason that as of May 15th you effectively would have been under the HVO Mostar Municipal Staff and that they, this -- this body, this organ who had replaced the Crisis Staff would have been responsible for your payment, for your salary, for the upkeep of the equipment?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a good observation, and I'm very happy that it was you who observed that, that it wasn't I myself who put that forward. But let me make things clearer. Let me repeat: The documents that I published in my book, I stand by those with -- before God and people that they are truthful, and you can see in the signatory, and Roko Markovina is a live witness, Saban Muratovic, we have live witnesses to testify to that. The other names don't matter, I'll remember them in due course. But as I say, it wasn't I myself who made those orders and decisions, it was they who wrote that down. You can see clearly the civilian protection stamp, and everything that happened happened between the 18th and 22nd of April. The fact that I did not know that any change had taken place, that they -- the people who should have informed me are to blame because they didn't inform me, as commander of the unit, of the development of events. And I repeat, you can read that in the book and the documents that are included there, my first orders or, rather, my first decisions at my own personal request when I asked to be issued order for my dismissal stating the reasons, because nobody ever did that. So if you follow the dates, then you'll be able to see when this Crisis Staff that you're talking about began to function. And let me repeat, that on the 30th of June, the civilian authorities withdrew and the military authorities took control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're going to get to that. We're going to get to that period, just step-by-step. The civilian protection, is that a volunteer organ or is that part of the community, you know, services?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. It's an organ which had to exist through force of law. It existed in peacetime, and it especially had to exist in that period of time, because it performs the function of civilian activities and it has its codes of conduct. It follows the United Nations codes and everything else which describes the function of a Civil Defence or civil protection organisation, whether they can use arms to shoot, whether they are allowed to bear arms. All that is defined in the code.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I take it, since it's defined by the code and by law, when serving in the civil protection, you get a salary?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bravo, sir. I received my last salary on the 18th of April, 1992, and the next salary on the 1st of September, 1995. So please remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not saying -- I'm not -- my question was in a broader nature. Normally, in times of peace, would you be receiving salary? Yes, no, or maybe.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, whether the civilian protection would pay it out or the firm, there were cases of both types in peacetime, and the working collective would pay for the worker that was engaged by the civilian protection or fire brigade unit or whatever. You would receive a salary. And that's why I said that the last salary I received was on the 18th of April, and the next salary on the 1st of July.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: It was the 1st of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that entire unit of civil protection that I belonged to did not receive a salary in that interim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And the equipment that you would use, were you, being a member of the civil protection, were you required to purchase your own equipment or was that provided to you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was neither provided nor did we purchase it. We used the existing equipment that the fire brigade association of Mostar had. With one exception, that my colleagues the Pompiers sans Frontieres and others would bring in the equipment they had. So we had problems sometimes with our hoses and the connection device for the hoses and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But I guess the point that I'm trying to make is that this was equipment that was provided for you in order for you to do this service, which was the benefit of the community, and not you, yourself and your colleagues, had to go out and purchase it from your own monies.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I stated things very clearly. We did not purchase them nor did the civilian protection purchase it. It was equipment that was inherited or, rather, taken from the fire brigade association of Mostar, the vehicles and the equipment. It wasn't something that was purchased by either the civilian protection or anybody else. And if you want to be absolutely exact, I have the moral right to say that there 1982 to the beginning of the aggression in 1992, I spent part of my income in the volunteer fire brigade. I invested it into purchasing some vehicles, and during that period of time, sir, we bought three new trucks. That's when I speak of myself personally. But I placed myself in the context of the other members, so my answer is that we did not purchase the equipment but neither did the civilian protection. It was equipment taken from the fire brigade association of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you said from 1982 to 1992, this is when you purchased this equipment, you helped purchase this equipment.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part. Three new trucks, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And this was during peacetime?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if I could move on to another topic. I want to go over briefly some of the events that you describe in your book that you published in 1997. I believe it's "Flames Above Mostar" or "Fire Flames Above Mostar." That's the title of it, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It is "Tongues of Fire Above Mostar" is the title of my book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, it seems that I can't get much right today. All right.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To your detriment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. Sadly so. Now, from reading the book - and I didn't read it, my colleagues read it - it would appear - correct me if I'm wrong - that -- that there was some professional competitiveness or jealousy between the -- the professional firefighters and those who were sort of volunteer firefighters serving in the civil protection.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think you're right on that score.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no competition, no competitiveness at all, not in peacetime and especially not in wartime. I don't think that the firefighters were ever more united than they were during that period of time to put out the fires. So on that score you're really not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it could be so. I got the impression that you had written at times you wouldn't get the calls in order to respond, and you felt left out.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I'll settle for that. I'm trying to get you home, sir. Help me help you. All right. Now, the equipment was rather limited for both the professional firefighters as well as your unit; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depended on who had what. The fire-fighting company numbered 120 employees before it was financed by the communities of interest, the SIZs, as they were known, and then they would buy equipment, fire extinguishing devices, and so on and so forth, which is quite logical because it was a unit that would go out first to intervene when the need arose. When there was a large-scale fire outside or on industrial plants and so on, they would ask for the volunteer fire brigade or the fire brigade of Mostar, whose commander I was at that time, to go out and help them. And then we would raise our unit to the alert and we'd go and serve as reinforcements to our colleagues the other firefighters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, your unit was located on the left or the east bank; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is where the fire brigade of Mostar was located, where its headquarters were from the 1800s.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And the professional firefighters were on the -- on the west bank?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the western part of town, near Rudnik, near the market. I don't know how else to explain it to you. I don't know how familiar you are with Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And they both fall within the municipality of Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, as you indicated, and you corrected me, you left only the 11th of May, 1992, to the left side. I mean, you --

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And -- the right side. I'm sorry. You left from the left side to the right side. You went from east to west; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And this was two days before the east -- the east side was lost?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And probably due to the circumstances, the heavy fighting and what have you, you were compelled to leave your equipment back on the east side. At least, that's what you say in your book on page 24.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that part of the equipment remained, a water truck in which Hasalic Almir was killed, and then in the warehouse there was some fire-fighting equipment; some uniforms, hoses, some of it. I say "some" because we evacuated from there. We had a truck to transport equipment and personnel, so in order to be sure that we would cross over other safely because sniper had been shooting since early morning hours, we loaded up as much equipment as possible. That was one of the ways to protect ourselves, through that equipment, and the other reason was to get out as much equipment to the other bank in that truck because I assumed that we would get to work, we would get busy once we crossed to the other side. Let me tell you, we were divided into sectors. The operations unit, where we were, was -- where we were going to, was sector 1, and we specifically were sector 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So the answer to my question that you left behind much of your equipment, the answer to that question is yes, you left it behind on the east bank.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by "much." I said clearly that some equipment we transported. We tried to move as much as possible, at least the part that was mobile. As an illustration, let me tell you that we had a borrowed battery that we borrowed from the other fire-fighting equipment, and that was the first piece of equipment that I loaded up on the truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Isn't it a fact, sir, that when you went to the west side you had to borrow equipment from the professional fire-fighting company in order to function?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, there was no need for me to borrow any equipment. The equipment was given to us because we were moved to a new location. We only took the water truck because, as I told you, our water truck had been left behind the department store. One of our colleagues was killed there, and that water truck was out of order. So we only received a new water truck from the fire-fighting unit. As for the rest of the equipment, all of it was owned by fire-fighting association.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So I take it you stand by what you wrote in your book on page 28, that you -- that you took, for usage - we would say borrowed, or they lent you - one fire truck, which had a capacity of five cubic metres; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. It was a fire truck that they gave you to use. It was part of their equipment and they were letting you use it. The west side allowing the east side to have that equipment, correct? Because you needed to respond to fires as well.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are forgetting - and I mentioned this - that we were an integral part of that defensive system, and we were sector 6. It wasn't our decision. It was pursuant to somebody else's decision. And whoever issued that order probably did it for their own interests. I was not in a position to defend the east side at that time or the side where the Serbs were. On the contrary. At that particular moment, I was defending or protecting the west side, where the population was mixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're going to get to that issue about the integral part, the east side fire-fighting unit with the west side. But first, as I understand from, again, reading your book, page 34, you indicate that on June 17th, three days after the liberation of the left side, you went back with the -- with the delegation of the civil protection; correct? You went back to --

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Once again, I refer you to the order of Mr. Roko Markovina who at that moment was chief of staff. Pursuant to his order, Ismet Drljevic, myself, Musan Dziman [phoen] and Zevin Digic [phoen], and the fifth person - I don't remember his name - we crossed to the left side to see what was left of the equipment of the fire-fighting association as well as in two local communes in order to enable the work of civilian protection. However, I emphasise that this was done pursuant to the order of Roko Markovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as I understand, two days later you began working on the left bank. Again, that's on page 34. And a simple yes would do, unless you want to explain.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have much explanation to give. You are quite correct, but we also remained in the location of the students' hall and in the location where we were. We remained there until September of that same year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we could fast forward to May, 1993. According to your book, on page 46 you indicate that around the second half of May, 1993, you received, I believe you say, again a visit from the Friends of Firemen or Firemen Without Frontiers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, their first arrival was sometime in September of 1992. This is how they accidentally became acquainted with us. And as a result of that, they came with a convoy, with a water truck of 1.000 litres, and some fuel. And as I said, we used that truck only once.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, yesterday, you made a point right before the break to tell us that we needed to keep in mind the date May 3, 1993. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember very well and I can repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When we came back from the break, you made references to an earlier date which I believe was January 22nd. We will get to it. It had to do with an order or decision. You're shaking your head. Does that mean yes?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm confirming, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Good. Now, and as we know, in between the second half of May and May 3rd, there are some events that happen in -- on May 9, 1993, and you touched upon that a little bit. So we don't have to go into great detail.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you put a specific question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Absolutely. Absolutely. Well, on May 9th the conflict began in earnest between the two sides.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And so now a few days later, since we're talking about -- a week or so later, the second half of May, 1993, you're saying that a truck, or these Firemen Without Frontiers came and brought approximately 1.500 kilos of different medicine and huge amounts of food; correct? That's in your book, page 46 to 47.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you read this correctly. That's quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you also indicate that they brought one fire-fighting vehicle; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct again. Capacity of 1.000 litres, a mixed fire-fighting truck. They had to paint it white so that it could come as part of the UN convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, as I understand it, Sarajevo was under siege; right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So that vehicle could not have come from the -- from the east side; right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I never really considered it. There are many ways to reach Mostar. Don't deceive yourself. A lot of convoys came through Croatia at the time. I don't care where this vehicle came from. At the entrance into Mostar, they had to paint it white. It was red previously, and they wouldn't let it through. And once it was painted white, it was allowed in as part of the UN convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it if we were to read your book, you would be able to point out specifically, page and line, where in your book you say that the vehicle had to be painted white in order to be brought in by the UN. Is that in your book? And you make reference to this on page 46 to 47. I have a copy of your book if you want to refresh your memory and our memory as well. I can provide it. That's not in your book, sir, is it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dear sir, I'm not claiming that I have any sort of a paper proving that this vehicle belonged to the UN. I'm repeating, and I'm emphasising that this vehicle had been brought in by our colleagues. In order for it to be allowed into Mostar, it had to be painted white to look as part of the UN convoy. I think that they came in in one single convoy. There were seven or eight - I'm not sure - of UN vehicles, and one of them was this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, sir, I put to you - and please correct me if I'm wrong - that none of that information that you just gave us is in your book. Nothing about the UN convoy, nothing about this truck having to be painted white for it to look as if it was a UN vehicle. Nothing at all. And the point I'm making is, just to make sure that we're all clear, that that vehicle came from the west side only a few days after the conflict had broken out. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat: I didn't say from which side the vehicle came. It was quite logical that the only passage was from the western side. If you want me to be quite precise, that direction is from the Buna River, or from Capljina, or from the western part of town via Citluk, Ljubuski, and so on. There were different routes into Mostar going through Croatia. I would refer you to my colleagues. They know which route they took. Now, whether I wanted this or not, the fact is that the vehicle had to come in from the south. Now, as to whether it was possible for it to come in from the south, it would have to go through the Buna bridge or through Capljina and some other locations. It is not very likely that it came from the north, and there was no other third possibility. And it definitely didn't come in from the eastern side. I can assure you of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least, I don't think it was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And your answer to my earlier question, that it came through the west. Now, I want to go through some documents with you very quickly. You had indicated earlier that your unit, being the volunteer unit that was part of the civil protection, was an integral part of the professional fire-fighting unit. That's your understanding, and that's what you wish us to -- to take away here today; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said any such thing. Let me clarify once again. Our unit was an independent unit acting within the joint detachment of civilian protection. The party carrying out activities was the professional fire-fighting unit, because it had best equipment, best personnel. So they were the main bearers of activity, and that's why they had the sector 1 designation. And there were a total of six sectors. We were the sixth sector, but we never portrayed ourselves as a professional unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. I'm not suggesting that you were professional, though obviously you were all professionally trained, but as I understood your answer to an earlier question, you indicated that you were an integral part of the fire-fighting unit.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And of course, being volunteers, that -- your role came into play especially during the summer months, as I understand it, when Mostar can be very, very hot. In fact, it was reputed to be the hottest place in the former Yugoslavia during the summer months; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct -- or, rather, Mostar is a hot city, but once again you're going back to something that I said nothing about. You are now referring to a volunteer fire-fighting unit in peacetime, and I am telling you that it was an independent, autonomous fire-fighting unit which recruited volunteers but within its composition it had a professional office, which I headed as commander. It was within the professional fire-fighting association. So we had nothing to do with the professional part, nothing except for professional cooperation. We cooperated together when there were fires. And that was during peacetime. As for wartime, we were more closely linked to the professional fire-fighting detachment because, as I said to you, it had best equipment, best personnel, and naturally we were an integral part of that organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. And you were both within or came under the municipality of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had we been in another municipality, then it would have been a different matter, but we were in Mostar region.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So the answer to my question is yes. You see, I'm insisting on getting direct answers from you, sir, even though we're wasting time.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, don't try to push me about the time. I'm not an accused person here. I'm just a witness, and after I'm done here, I will go back home. You have to do your job, sir, I have to do my job, and it doesn't matter to me whether we're finished today or in five days. I'm a retiree, I have plenty of time, so please don't try to intimidate me. And you have attempted to do that several times. Thank you. I'm in no rush at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you would like to know what the exact status of this fire-fighting brigade was. I would like to intervene here. Could we please show the witness Exhibit number 4240, please. Registrar, could you please show this on the ELMO, please, P4240. Very well. Sir, this is a document which you have signed. Do you recognise your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... and I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, can you read out in your own language, which is what is on the top left-hand part above number 17. What is written here?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Professional fire-fighting unit, Mostar. Number 17. Date 17th of August, 1993."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a document which you have signed. You have the title of commander of a unit, and under the stamp we can read "Professional unit -- professional fire-fighting unit." If you were an independent unit, why did you not write "volunteers' unit" or "volunteer unit"? You said this. It's written here, it says, "Professional unit." And on reading this document, I think one can quite legitimately believe that your status was that of a professional fire-fighting unit. Maybe this is what Mr. Karnavas would like you to say. I must intervene here to gain some time. Why do you state here that this is a professional unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, please allow me to explain how this came about. It is true that at this point in time we were officially declared and appointed as Mostar's fire-fighting unit. Yesterday, in my evidence, I said so, but maybe it was overlooked, and I hope that it will be in the record now. Once the civilian authorities were established on the left bank in 1993, immediately after the beginning of the aggression, after the 9th of May, sometime in early July, you have to understand that until that time there was just military rule, military authorities, until July, and then sometime in July, or maybe late June, civilian authorities were established and they wanted to create civilian structure, and as part of that, they established us as a professional fire-fighting unit and they also established the work organisation called water utility, or waterworks. I explained that yesterday. So these are two civilian associations established at that time by civilian authorities. Thus, it was logical for me to send this information to the civilian protection staff. Unfortunately, the colleague who worked on this letter didn't record that this information was sent to civilian protection staff and the War Presidency, because via this letter I informed them about the problems with tyres, fuel, batteries, personnel; all the things that we needed. So you're quite right, this title is a full one and is a correct one, and this was our title. And to this day this unit is known under this title, professional fire-fighting unit of Mostar. That's the explanation, and I hope you will take it into account. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Karnavas, I don't know whether I could help you at all. Another Judge is going to lend you some assistance as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, I can understand that you feel somehow pressured. I intervene as someone who does not come from the American system but knows it a bit, and it is in fact possible to ask you to answer a question by just yes or no, and you should not take this as an offence. I sort of testify that this is really correct. And please do not feel that you are attacked. This may be a bit of a courtroom game, but it is not really, I think, a bad intention of Mr. Karnavas nor of any other lawyer when they ask you to say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we could -- I would like to show you the first document. It's 1D00389. I will need some assistance. This is my first time with this new e-court system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we please have all the cross-examination exhibits released to the Prosecution at this time so we have access to these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The answer to that question, Your Honour, is no, we will do it one by one. I may choose not to show any documents. We went through this argument yesterday. I believe the case on this issue is closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, my request was not to Mr. Karnavas. My request was for the assistance of the Chamber and for a ruling from the Chamber, regardless of what Mr. Karnavas's position is. It's only fair that we now have -- the witness has completed his direct examination. We can have no influence on him whatsoever. He is under oath. We can't talk to him, and it's only fair that we now have the documents. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Karnavas, we're going to make a ruling on the issue of whether this document should be disclosed 24, 48 hours in advance or a week before. But this is not the issue here at stake. You remember the decisions I have already issued. We have to have a hard copy of the exhibits, of the documents, in the language of the witness and also in English. You give me one copy of it, and you give one copy to the Prosecution so that they can look at it from all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well -- well, Your Honour Mr. President, again I want to apologise. I'm not as smooth as I normally would like to be. I have made four copies. I did not make a hard copy for the Prosecutor. Until -- until a formal ruling is made, however, on this -- just this one occasion, I'm willing to break my own personal rules and provide the Prosecution with everything. I don't want to take advantage of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if you could look at this document, sir. And it would appear from the very top we see a date, and the date is 25 July, 1992. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And above that we can see that this is from the municipality of Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you have a look at the heading, you can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And if you -- if you could just take a second or two to read it.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Decision on pooling the equipment of the volunteer fire brigade unit and the equipment of the professional fire brigade unit. "The equipment of the volunteer fire brigade shall be pooled and joined to the equipment of the professional fire brigade unit. "This decision shall enter into force on the date that it was adopted."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, it would appear, at least from the documents that I've been able to glean at, that this was the first date, 25 July, 1992, that your unit was asked to be integrated with the professional fire unit. Would you agree that that's what this document appears to be saying, that there's a decision made by the president of the HVO of the municipality of the Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course that's not in dispute, but this is in fact an order, not a decision. The official title is "Decision," but it's in fact an order. We never received this order or decision because I was replaced before this decision on the 15th of July, 1992, and then this decision was issued. And I can say this for sure. But it's quite obvious that I can't deny the contents of this decision. But we never received it, because I would have been proud to publish it in my book. And on the 15th of July I was replaced, as I've already said, and that was ten days prior to this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, we're going to go step-by-step, but I just want to make sure that we are all on the same page. This is a decision from the Croatian Defence Council of the municipality of Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And since you're telling us today -- and at the bottom you see the name Jadran Topic, and that was the Topic you were referring to yesterday; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That relates to the decision that I published.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. And since you're telling us today that you were unaware of this decision, since had you been aware of it you would have been proud to put it in your book, it's fair to say that you could not have complied with this decision if you were not aware of it; right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct, because at the time the equipment had already been pooled with that of the professional fire brigade unit. I had already been replaced, a new commander appointed, and to be quite frank, at that time he would go to the meetings of unit commanders. But as to the orders he received as and to the way that he conducted himself, well, that was his personal affair, because for the next year he was in fact the commander of the unit. As of the 15th of July, up until July, 1993, roughly speaking, this man was the unit commander, and he received orders, executed and implemented the orders. That was his affair.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, maybe I -- I was inarticulate in my question. This order was never complied with, whether you were aware of it or not, was it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've said that it was complied with, because the equipment had already been pooled. The equipment was joint equipment, because the fire truck is one we held onto. We continued to do our work. The unit hadn't been withdrawn at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I -- I'm a little confused because of your comments yesterday on the document that was shown to you by the Prosecutor - and that was 65 ter number 9511 - that was the January 22, 1993, decision. That's the one that you indicated had you complied with that decision, then obviously the east side would not have had a fire unit during the early May activities. So there seems to be some sort of a contradiction, but perhaps I just simply misunderstood you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll repeat what I said. We did not execute the order or the request dated the 22nd or 23rd of January. That's correct. And I told you why we didn't comply with that order. As for this order, I won't deny that the order existed. I was replaced ten days prior to the order. At the time, I didn't even know whether I was still a member of the fire brigade or not. I didn't know whether I was a civilian or not. So I wasn't on duty for ten days. I hadn't been on duty for 10 days at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And just to make sure that -- I want to clarify this point. I'm not suggesting that you personally refused to comply with the order. But in any event, if we could go to another document, and that would be 1D00388. If we could look at that document. And again I apologise for the awkwardness of this presentation. It's my first time. If you could just look at it first. Take your time, look at it. And if you need assistance to have the document moved up or down a little bit, and I think in the future -- okay. It may be more beneficial to also provide you with a hard copy. This document is dated 16 September, 1992, is it not, sir?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it would appear that this again is a decision.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: A decision of the Croatian Defence Council, municipality of Mostar, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And this particular decision, it says right at the very beginning, at the preamble, if you want, or right below it, that it's a decision "On creating municipality administration structures for fire protection, professional fire brigade of Mostar." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that quite clearly. I can see the contents of the decision. It's really not necessary for me to read it through, I'm familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. It would appear, at least, that here the municipality of Mostar is trying to consolidate or create -- recreate the professional fire brigade of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to be precise, on the 16th of September, 1992, a decision was taken on forming a professional fire-fighting company. In order to change the name, and only to change the name, and I'm emphasising this fact, the name was Professional fire-fighting Brigade, but only to change the name, because the unit didn't receive anything new, it was necessary to organise a professional fire-fighting unit, the Mostar professional fire-fighting unit, and that was on the 16th of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And would that also include incorporating, sort of, the volunteer unit? Or if you tell us they were already incorporated from the previous document.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, if we could go to another document, and this is 1D00390. And this is an unofficial -- this is the original one, and we have an unofficial translation. If you could look at that. Take your time. I know the letters are kind of small, but perhaps they could enlarge them for you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can see the text quite clearly. It's the document that I published in my book. It says that the equipment has to be made available to the professional fire-fighting company and the staff of the volunteer brigade shall be placed at the disposal according to need. It means that the unit should be dismantled and the equipment should be provided to the company. It means that the volunteer fire-fighting unit no longer exists. You take its equipment, you dismiss its staff, and as a result the unit no longer exists. So the decision is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, are you sure that this is in your book, sir? Perhaps you could be mistaken.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, you're mistaken, or yes, it's in your book? It was a compound question. It was ill-phrased on my part. This is not in your book, sir, is it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you're quite right. I apologise. The date here is a different one, but the contents are probably the same. In January we received a document with the same contents. I do apologise to the Court and to you yourself, but the text is identical. It was reproduced. It's the same text as the one that we have in the decision that we received. Our decision was taken on the 22nd of January, and we received it on the 28th of January, whereas the date of this document is different. But the text is identical to the text of the previous decision, it's just the date that differs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Needless to say, if we look at the date, 17 of September, 1992, the whole purpose of this decision is to try consolidate and incorporate.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not 1993, but in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 1992. November, 1992; correct? You shook your head. Does that mean yes, sir, for the record?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then if we go to the following document, and that was the document that was presented by the Prosecution to you, and I believe this document might have been in your book --

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The text is identical. There is no different. I will repeat this: It's only the dates that are different. Here the date is the 17th of December, and our decision was dated the 23rd of January. And I can claim with full responsibility that we received this decision on the 28th. So one month later, a little over a month later, we received the decision, but the text is identical. If you have a look, you can see for yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we're going to get to that. Now, the next document, which I failed to mention, that's the OTP document from -- it's 9511. That was the 65 ter number. And since you mentioned it, and perhaps we can bring that up on the screen, since you mentioned it, these decisions appear to be virtually the same, one could conclude, perhaps, that at least the earlier decision, the November decision, that is, had not -- had not been implemented as of January 22, 1993, which was why it was necessary to issue another decision. Would that be fair to conclude?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat what I've already said. We received the order on the 28th, the order on how to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, there was a decision back on November 17, 1992. Let me ask you concretely: Do you know for a fact whether that decision was implemented? Yes or no. Did the volunteer fire -- I'm sorry. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It couldn't have been implemented if we didn't have the decision on that date. We received the document on the 28th of January, 1993. We never received the decision dated the 17th of November, 1992. We could only have implemented the decision after we had received it. Up until the 22nd of January, we weren't aware of the decision. Even if we wanted to comply with the decision, we wouldn't be able to because we knew nothing about it. But when we received it on the 28th, once we had this decision in our hands, we refused to comply with the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what I'm suggesting, sir, and what I put to you, sir, is that there was no intention of complying with this order back in 17 November, 1992, because these are two different decisions, and that perhaps you are in error when you state here today that the decision of 17 November, 1992, had not been received.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You're completely wrong. The text is identical but the date is different. And you can see this in this decision too. In our decision it says the 22nd of January, and I claim with full responsibility that it wasn't until the 28th that we received the decision. But let's not quarrel about dates. If we had received it on the 17th of December, we wouldn't have executed the order, just as we didn't executed the order on the 28th of January. That would have meant handing over the entire fire brigade in Mostar to the company. It would mean dismantling the unit. No one had the power to do it apart from the Assembly of that association. It could only have been done because of specific conditions, and that's -- that's the truth, because it wasn't a non-governmental organisation that was part of the civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it that what you're suggesting here today is that the municipality of Mostar did not have the authority to consolidate its resources during this time right after having survived an attack, and it's trying to put its city back together. Is that what you're suggesting?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat this: The Mostar fire brigade could only be dismantled if the Assembly of the association took such a decision. It's only that organisation that had the authority. The authorities in town had to make such a proposal to the association, but it's only the association of the Mostar fire brigade that had the power to suggest and -- to suggest that the unit should be dismantled and to actually dismantle the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm lost for time. I don't know when we're supposed to take our next break, and I have three more documents. I don't want to get into another document if we're about to take our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're going to take have break. How much time do you need still on this issue of the firefighters? I fail to see the relevance of your questions, but maybe if one question is put to the witness we will be enlightened, but I still fail to see what your purpose is, but you probably have an objective. It may come to the fore later on. Let's hope so. Now, it is -- how much time do you need after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Since we're making some progress, Your Honour, I would suspect no more man 20 minutes, 25 at the most, perhaps even less. I will try and I can assure the Judges and Your Honour that there are points that are being made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's hope so. It is now ten past twelve. Fifteen-minute break. We shall resume at 25 past twelve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Please proceed, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, I had three documents, I'm down to two. I put one aside. Perhaps we can go through them rather quickly. This is 1D00392. If you'd just give it a quick glance. This is a decision that's dated 22 January, 1993. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in this particular decision, there's an appointment of the commander of the professional fire brigade of Mostar, and that's Mr. Babic; right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is the same date as the other decision that you discussed with the Prosecutor on direct and we briefly touched upon; right? Those two decisions came on that same day. At least, it would appear from --

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were probably written on the same day, but the date is the 22nd of January, 1993, and that means that they discussed these matters at the same time and at the same session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if I could go to the next document very quickly. That's the OTP 65 ter document 9512. This was a decision again, dated 3 May, 1993, touched upon by the Prosecutor. You commented on it, and I just want to briefly go over this. I'm being corrected by my colleague here that this is a letter, actually, as opposed to a decision. I stand corrected. But nonetheless, you see this, do you not?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And this is actually -- this letter is from the civilian protection; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it would appear that as a result of the non-compliance of the previous decisions, the ones that I mentioned earlier, which are dated back as early as November, 1992, this letter --

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite likely. I wouldn't dispute that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And so with this letter, basically it would appear that the two fire-fighting units part company.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with that. Have a look at the decision on forming the professional fire-fighting unit. Have a look on the decision on appointing a fire-fighting unit commander, and you will see that nowhere is the volunteer fire-fighting unit mentioned nor is its status mentioned. This is only mentioned in the decision of the 22nd of January, 1993, and since the order wasn't executed, then it is quite logical to expect a letter such as this one. I would have expected such a reaction, because as I have already said, we really did not comply with the order or, rather, the decision dated the 22nd of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Exactly. That was my point, and you put it much more artfully than I had phrased the question, though I had indicated that it would appear, at least, from the documents that we have seen that the non-compliance went back as early as November 17, 1992. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We differ on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. We differ on that point. We will agree to disagree. But I put to you, sir - perhaps this is the point that I've been trying to make, perhaps not as successfully as I had hoped - was that the decisions that were -- that if we look at these documents in sequence, we see that the municipality of Mostar is attempting to consolidate the fire-fighting units; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in terms of forming and organising a professional fire-fighting unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And at some point decisions are issued which are not complied?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat what I have said: We didn't comply with the decision. I have told you why. We didn't receive the decision dated the 17th of November. That's the first reason. It wasn't until the 22nd of January that we received the following decision, which we refused to comply with, because it stated quite clearly that the equipment would be pooled or, rather, handed over to the professional fire-fighting company, and it stated that the unit would be dismantled. That meant that the unit and its equipment would no longer exist and that is the essence of that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But I put to you, sir, that these decisions have nothing to do with the events of May 9, 1993.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's leave that to the historians. That's for the historians to investigate. You and I shouldn't go into that, and we shouldn't tire the Chamber with such matters either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. Okay. Now, just a couple of other matters. You were effectively demoted, were you not, as early as 13 June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was the 13th of July, but I do know that it was in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. July. And this was 1992?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it this must have been sort of a painful shock to you, given your -- the services that -- that you had given, the dangers that you had faced. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with that. Allow me to explain this very briefly. I wasn't hurt by the decision to replace me. I was hurt by the fact that I didn't know what to do after having been replaced, because I was just a clay -- a clay pigeon then, and there was an oral order that we -- that you are not aware of, but according to that order, I was no longer allowed to drive and use a fire-fighting vehicle, and if I was on duty, I wasn't allowed to communicate with my colleagues. So please take that into consideration. This did hurt me. I was left in an unprotected area, in an open area, and it was a long time before oral decision was taken with regard to my dismissal. And in that decision it stated that I was a member of the unit of civilian protection. That's what hurt me, because I didn't know what would happen to me. But no one can remain in a certain position forever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything is temporary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And when you were replaced, at least from the name that you provided us yesterday, it would appear that you were replaced with a -- by a Muslim; is that correct? A younger man, someone --

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. A younger man, ten years younger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in fact, if I understand correctly what you have stated, there had been some sort of a debate of putting a Croat, but it was the Muslims that objected and ultimately that's -- they chose that individual who was younger and perhaps less experienced, not as wise as you, to -- to fill that position; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that the proposal was for Miroslav Mrdja, that particular name, to be the commander of the unit instead of Meho Kekic. However, two people from the Bosniak ethnic group were against that. They were members of the civilian protection staff and their view was upheld and Mr. Kekic was appointed. But if you're talking about years, then Miroslav Merdzo was a lot younger than Meho Kekic, let alone me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And do those two individuals who were on the civil protection staff, were they members of the SDA party, by any chance?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think either of them were members of any party, to the best of my knowledge. And to be quite frank, that would be my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I just have a few more questions. At some point there was a formation of a civilian government on the -- on the east side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in July 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it was about that time when the city, effectively, at least from a governance point of view, was divided. You had two governments; one for the west and one for the east.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. And you needn't think the situation is better now either. Everything is relative, after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I'd rather not comment on the present. And it was during this period when the fighting was going on, the sniping back and forth, the shelling back and forth?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it - and I mean this very sincerely - that this entire period for you personally must have been a very difficult period, being caught in the middle of all of this.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite frank, it was a difficult period because the situation was so complex. You had no food, no supplies, no water. There was shelling all the time, and for purposes of illustration, let me tell you that it's about 800 metres from my house to the fire brigade. And if I tell you, sir, that I had to run across the street in five places not to be killed by a sniper, then you can use this to see what the situation was like. So only 800 metres, and I had to rush across in five places to save my head. If you walked slowly, you'd be killed off just like a pigeon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. But it must have been difficult, you being a Serb, when you had the JNA or the Serbs attacking the town and then you had the two warring factions, and there you are, caught in the middle, trying to find your own space even though you had lived in Mostar for generations, you and your family.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you want me to be quite frank, I never felt safer as relationships between one man to another. And you must remember that. I never felt safer one man with another. There were certain hooligans, if I can put it that way, not to use a worse term, who tried to attack my house and my wife, and it was the Bosniaks that stopped them, the Bosniaks that occupied important positions in town and protected myself and my house. And never again to the present day did anything like that repeat itself. And that's the truth of it. So I never felt safer from that point of view than I did then, because an enormous number of people knew me, they knew me before the war, and they knew how to value and respect all the things that I had done. I was -- this is -- I was fairly well recognised, even if I say so myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in spite of all of that, when you showed up with a walkie-talkie that one night, your own friends and neighbours questioned your motives for having that walkie-talkie with you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And I said who those people were, and I said why they wanted to check me out. Perhaps I forgot to say in all this that my wife is a Croat. So that was one other unfavourable element in respect of the environment I lived in, because most of the population living around me were Serbs. The majority were Serbs there in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. I appreciate our exchange. I trust you won't hold it against me for maybe pushing you too hard, and I wish you a fair journey back to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. Do you want documents to be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could reserve my -- and wait until the conclusion of all of the questioning, Your Honour, if that's okay. On the Defence side, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you please. We have another hour left. Who is the next counsel for cross-examination? Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I hope that I will get through my cross-examination quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pejanovic, good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: My name is Senka Nozica, and I am Defence counsel for Mr. Bruno Stojic. I would first of all like to ask you something about your relationships with your colleagues, and -- from the western side or western bank. Let's say during 1992, when you crossed over to the west bank, to and including the events of the 9th of May, 1993, that you mentioned, when your colleagues found themselves in no-man's land in between and you went to look for them. Can we say that the relationships between you and your colleagues the firefighters were highly proper?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, highly proper, and I say that with full responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You explained to us the event of the 9th of May, 1993, when you went to look for your colleagues who found themselves somewhere in the vicinity of the Bristol Hotel in Santica Street. And as far as I remember, you said that they joined you for a certain amount of time until the situation was right for them to go back.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. They shared our food and our beds and any cigarettes we received. You can be quite sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Can we also observe that that was the fact during the period of time when you were all on the right bank and when you were divided into sectors, as you said? Was there any animosity or did they have full trust and confidence in you that in your sector you would do what was necessary, and was your unit confident towards them? Did they have confidence in them?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, thank you for asking me that question. I would love my colleagues to be here as well, especially Mr. Vlado Babic, who until recently was the commander of that professional fire brigade unit. I think he would be best placed to explain this to you. Allow me to be a little immodest and say that none of my colleagues from the volunteer unit or, rather, the unit that I had in a way established, none of my colleagues from the professional fire brigade either had a single bad word to say to me or about me because they never had any reason to do so, because I never did anything that I should be ashamed of or for anybody to look at me askance. So let me say this as well: I'm perhaps one of the let's say 100 -- I'm one of a hundred or a thousand people who very early on obtained permits by the European Union, and I now have here in my pocket, if that means anything to you, an UNPROFOR card. Of 1.500 people, I am one of the bearers of this card, gentlemen. The number is 145, so I was among the first 145 people to be issued this permit and card allowing me to cross over into the other part of town. I apologise for having to say "into the other part of town," but this is the document that I was able to use. And it's a very dear keepsake for me, to go in an armoured escort and so on and so forth. You know what it meant to have a card like this. And I also received a card of the European Union, and very early on I began crossing over. Actually, straight after the conflict ceased, and even at the time when, in inverted commas, the border was at Hit, by the Hit department store, when you had to have special permits signed by the heads of the MUP services on both sides in order to cross over. So I was able to cross over, and I swear to you that never throughout that time did I ever encounter anybody saying a single ugly word to me, let alone an incident or anything like that taking place. And I'm very proud of that and very happy of that for that reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Yes, I know that. And let us conclude for the Trial Chamber that you were a very well-known personage throughout Mostar. So when you said that nobody ever uttered a bad word to you or said anything ugly to you, on the right side everybody knew who you were, that you were doing your duty, doing your professional business.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm going ask you something else now. During your testimony yesterday, you spoke about the destruction of Orthodox churches on the left bank, and you said, asked by the Prosecutor -- when asked which Orthodox churches were destroyed -- the Prosecutor in fact asked you this on page 63, line 16, which Orthodox churches were damaged or destroyed in 1993. That was what he asked you. Now, can you tell me, please, Karadzoz-bey mosque, for instance, was it damaged in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was. I remember that full well. The 11th of May, when I set out towards my own home and the point in time when I decided to cross over to the other side, I saw that the bestiality that was going on there, you couldn't survive. And when I was approaching my house, my Serb neighbours were packing up their things and leaving town with their families, and the message was clear to me, loud and clear, that somebody like me, thinking like I thought, had nothing to do there any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, please spoke more slowly. It's a bit hard to follow you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. On my way home, I saw the minaret of the mosque, that it had been toppled, and as I said, the round point there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the 11th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I can now go back to something I was asking you about the Orthodox churches. How many Orthodox churches were there in eastern Mostar at that time?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question is a little more specific now and I'll try and answer more specifically. I was speaking of two churches yesterday; the cathedral church, which is right above the main road, the M17 main road, motorway, and I spoke about the old church, or Stara Crkva, which is about 100 metres or 150 metres above the cathedral church. And it has very deep foundations so that you have to get right up close to the church in order in order to see it. It's dug into the ground. So that the -- those are the two churches in the urban area. But if you look at the broader area of Mostar, then the church in Bijelo Polje was set fire to. It was devastated, and the bell tower and bell was taken away. I can also say that Sipamisa monastery [phoen] was wholly set on fire and blown apart.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm asking you this, sir, because in your statement you said that in the eastern part of town there were two churches. Yesterday, when asked by the Prosecutor, you went into an explanation of the fact that one church was set on fire and then destroyed by the HOS or HVO, not to go back to that. Now, I'd like ask you, can you tell me about this other church, the other church that was along the M17 motorway. Was that destroyed? How was that destroyed?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really know. We don't have a report on the fire that was caused on that church. We just registered it as a fire, but we don't have the actual informational report that came in about that church. That is the old church that was set on fire and which burnt down. The one along the M17 motorway was first of all set on fire and then blown up.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In your statement to the Prosecutor, you make some assumptions as to who could have set that church on fire. Now, I'm just asking you if you remember, and in view of the population composition, the residents living near the church, who would that be?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think I gave my assumptions. However, I have to say that around the church itself at that point in time there was an open space, a wide-open space. All the residential buildings, the old ones, had been set fire to, and all the buildings that were built without permits on the northern side of the church wall were not inhabited because in 80 per cent of the cases they were houses belonging to Serbs from the Nevesinje area. They had started constructing these new houses. But as they did not have a permit to do so, construction work stopped and then the war broke out, so at that time there was nobody living there and it was a wide-open space.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you tell us what your assumptions were as to who set the church on fire, what you told the Prosecutor, and was that in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was, in July 1992, and my assumption was that this was perpetrated by HOS, the HOS, and I deduced that on the basis of many stories and rumours going round and talks I had. Now, who set the explosives there, who blew it up I don't know, but a man who didn't know I was coming here nor that I had been asked to give a statement of any kind told me, "You'll get a picture from me, a photograph from me of the -- when your church was blown up." Now, what he had in mind, I don't know, I can give you his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, that's not important. It seems that we have not understood each other or, rather, maybe we have. Let me ask you, what do you mean when you refer to the old church? Is that the assumption you made about who had mined the old church?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have no assumptions as to who destroyed the old church because we don't have a report about the fire that broke out there. Now, in view of the times that we lived through and the times when this happened, because this was probably done before Christmas, 1993 --

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 1993. There is a high probability that the perpetrators were the forces of the Bosniak people. I'm not saying that for certain, but there is great probability that that is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. That's what you said. And I just wanted to check out whether you stand by what you said on that occasion. Now, I will turn to something else, and I have just one question. I will enumerate bridges in Mostar, and I will ask you to tell me only in which year they were destroyed. We don't need to go into details, we don't need to go into speculation. I'm just interested in the year, I'm not interested in who destroyed bridges. What about Lucki bridge? Do you know where it is?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It was destroyed in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tito's bridge in Musala?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Same. Same year. I don't know whether it was before or after, but it was same year.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The bridge of Ivo Lola Ribar, or Carinski bridge?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Same. I was in the yard of the hospital when it was mined. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Ivo Lola Ribar. Lola is the nickname - I'm saying this for the record - and it was also known as Carinski bridge. Not Zarinski but Carinski. So your answer remains the same, 1992?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Zeljeznicki bridge, or Sutina bridge.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Same year.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Zeljeznicki, or Sutina bridge. What about the bridge of Hasan Brkic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Same year.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Aviator's bridge, or Military bridge?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Same year.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Zeljeznicki bridge in the industrial zone of the town.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the bridge towards the aluminum, linking the left bank with the right one. Same year.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. I think that there was another bridge.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me add, there was a bridge in Vojno at the axis into Mostar. It was destroyed the same year. Then there's a bridge in Zitomislici. I think it was towards the end of 1991. More likely that than early 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The bridge in Zitomislici, that's missing in the transcript. Zitomislici. That's the last bridge that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The last bridge in a series of bridges, and it belonged to Mostar municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm insisting on the record. I asked that it be entered in the record: Zitomislici. This bridge also was in Mostar municipality.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. But there's a distinction there. The right bank belonged to Citluk municipality and the left bank, where Zitomislici is, was Mostar municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for the supplement. So the first bridge is by the petrol station, and then the next one is in Zitomislici.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I have just two more brief questions. Yesterday you spoke about the valve. You said that most likely - this was your assumption - most likely it was not in order and could not be shut down completely, and due to this fortunate circumstance, you still had water on the other bank. Did you know at the time where that valve was, on which side?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was clearly on the right bank. That's more than certain. I don't know the exact location.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I have just one more question. Yesterday, you mentioned this, and I don't want to go into great detail because my colleagues might explore this, but yesterday you spoke about a fire which broke out on the 23rd of August, 1993, in the residential building called Beirut. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You spoke about what would have happened to the driver had he not left the vehicle or the area because of the lighter. Tell me this: Based on your opinion, was the HVO able to see fire-fighting trucks there?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not a chance, because the fire had been caused before we got there. Since the shelling continued, it just so happened that this driver happened to be there, and there was this comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So we can conclude that when this shell was fired, or when it landed, because not a lot of time lapses in between, the HVO was unable to see your fire-fighting truck?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a chance. There wasn't a chance for anybody to see it, because one vehicle was in the passage so that it was completely invisible. And the other vehicle was so close to the building that there was no chance anybody could have seen it. Even if they stood above the truck, they could not have fired the shell and ensure that it would land where it landed. It was just a pure coincidence, pure chance.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've concluded, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in order to be economical with time, it seems that we are quite under time pressure, and I don't want to be prejudicial to my client. My client wanted to put seven to eight questions to this witness of a military nature related to some of the topics that this witness touched upon in his evidence. I would like to ask that this opportunity be given to my client, and based on your ruling, I can then tailor my cross-examination to that situation. So I would first like my client to be given an opportunity to put questions and then I will proceed. Thank you Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Praljak, you are authorised for a period of ten minutes to ask eight questions of a military nature.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
