utterances.text: Mr. Pejanovic, thank you for answering my questions. In view of the limited amount of time, would you please answer with yes, no, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You pointed to the hills; Hum, Brkan's hill, and others. In 1992, was the JNA positioned there?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On Hum hill, yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Was Mostar surrounded by the JNA at that time from all sides?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, mostly. Well, you can't say from all sides because they were not on the right bank.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: The road leading across Goranci, was that the only road leading into Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Road of Salvation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did many people die there?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very many people, because the curve had been shot at.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that in May there was an operation of the HVO liberating the right bank of the Neretva up until the aluminum plant Soko?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. This was when Orilovac [phoen] was seized.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know who commanded that operation?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that in June of that year -- rather, in May of 1992, on the 13th everybody was expelled from the left bank, mostly everybody, and directed to the right bank? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that was true. I myself left on the 11th.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. When people were fleeing across the Tito's bridge, people were jumping into the Neretva River, did many die there?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the bridge itself, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that in June the HVO, with a lot of Muslims being members of the HVO unit, liberated Mostar by crossing the Neretva in four locations and that that was in June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know who commanded that action?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My respect to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that as a result of that we have precise information as to who or which members of the army took part in that liberation?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that you do have such information.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In the hills on the east side of Mostar, did the army of Republika Srpska remain there?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Podvelezje area.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: In Podvelezje and all the way up to Stolac.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that region less but I know this based on the stories that I heard, that they had positions there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So in 1992 in May and June, the HVO, as an organised army at the time, liberated Stolac and that whole area leading all the way up to above Mostar.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And prior to that, all civilians had been deported to the right bank.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Did this involve several tens of thousands of people?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A large number of people were deported or expelled. Some of them left with the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, another set of questions. When you stand in the area where your headquarters was, the area where your colleague was killed, when you stand at the zebra crossing and at the corner that you showed to us, and as you face the west, the western direction, would you be able to see the Glas bank, that building?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly only the top of that building but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. After the cessation of hostilities, did you go to the elevator where you supposed that the sniper was?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never entered that bank building.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So would you be able to see the area where the people were wounded, killed, and where a pigeon was killed?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never entered the bank building so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. You put out a fire in a location in the vicinity of the Neretva, and you said yesterday that most likely the sniper shot from the building of the high school.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I'm claiming that firmly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Can you see from that area the high school?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, both the building and the windows, and I'm positive about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. Do you know that a Chinese-made multiple rocket launcher, do you know whether it was behind the hill or on the hill?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I'm not an artilleryman, so I truly don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: It was behind. Did you see when the shells were fired and you spoke about the southern part of Mostar --

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it involves Blagaj --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: No. Did you see the firing?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as relating Blagaj, I didn't see the firing. I heard they hit land.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did you see the missiles flying?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as they were flying above our heads.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, before they hit the ground.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that only by means of a ballistic expertise can one establish where any kind of missile comes from?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I never considered that. It wasn't important for my book. I just wanted to describe what had happened there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you distinguish a rifle from a sniper? What's the difference between them?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd say that a sniper has a softer firing sound.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So -- thank you. A sniper and a rifle differ only --

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In optic sight.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know how atmospheric pressure, speed of wind, or any other such elements affect the trajectory of a missile?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's all I had, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I know a lot about submarine missiles and submarine artillery missiles because I studied that when I was in the JNA for 24 months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I'll try to be very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please try to do like Mr. Praljak and see if things will move ahead much faster.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pejanovic, good afternoon. My name is Bozidar Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm representing Mr. Praljak, who used up his right to put some questions to you himself.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And I think that because of that we proceeded more quickly. I have several things I'd like to cover with you. I hope to be brief, but I will kindly ask you, whenever possible, to answer with a yes or a no so that we can proceed quickly. There's no point in repeating what you said yesterday or earlier today. It's already in the transcript. Let me ask you some minor things initially. Yesterday, on the map that you marked quite a lot, it's marked as PD --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: -- and at one point you were supposed to mark with letters A, B, C, and D some locations, namely the hills around Mostar. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, and I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If you wish, we can put the map on the ELMO but, rather, you have it in front of you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: These marks A, B, C, and D, you drew them on the very edge but locations themselves are not portrayed on the map.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said right away that the map is not big enough to show these locations that's why I only roughly indicated where these features are located around Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I have a question for you, and just answer with yes or no. These locations, Hum and others, they are not shown on this map.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I just pointed the direction where they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. You described the incident on the source of the Buna river, where Tekija is. I have just one minor detail to ask you about that. The missiles, there were two missiles, they hit the hill?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were there any military positions there?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Any other significant facilities?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Underneath was Tekija and the source of Buna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: How far from there?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we're talking about 150 to 200 metres down. This is the difference in elevation. It is not horizontal distance, and it's about hundred metres from where the missiles landed down to the source of the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you conclude, based on anything, that these missiles targeted precisely the Tekija building?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's nothing else of interest in that area at all, no positions whatsoever, nothing populated, no people. That was the only facility, the only thing that existed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, you think that because you didn't see anything there yourself, you didn't see any other facilities, you are assuming --

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not assuming. I'm claiming there is nothing else in the vicinity, in the vicinity where the missiles landed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right, let's take it apart. You are sure there are no facilities there.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there are no facilities there whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And are you sure that these missiles targeted precisely Tekija?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't claim that. I wouldn't dare to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: There has been a lot of discussion of the water system in eastern Mostar, and I think we need to go back to that because legally that is quite relevant. First of all, please tell me, during this conflict from May 1993 and on, was the situation with water supply on the western part of Mostar better?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. You said that the water supply network actually was damaged back in 1992.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when the bridges were mined.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You said that on page 92. I'm just saying this for the purposes of the record. You said this on page 72 and 74 of the transcript. And this is what appears in your testimony, after certain improvisations were made in order to join up hoses.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were bypasses that were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Who made those bypasses?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were members of the civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So this was while HVO had civilian authority in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So we can say it was while HVO was in power?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You just nodded for the sake of the transcript. You have to say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you not too tired? Can you continue your testimony, sir? Are you all right? Are you feeling all right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you give us an approximate idea of when the municipal authorities created those temporary bypasses?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately after the Serbs had withdrawn. I think it was perhaps in the first half of July. Not all the crosses were dealt with at the same time, so it was in the first half of July that the first bypasses were made.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let's take this step-by-step. I'll put a direct question to you. I put it to you that all this appears a little absurd. First the Serbs -- or, rather, I apologise, the JNA, the reservists, destroyed the bridges. I'm not referring to the Serbian people. They first destroyed the bridges, they destroyed the water supply system, they destroyed other forms of infrastructure that had been discussed. The HVO expelled them from the area. The HVO reconstructed, rebuilt what they could, given the conditions. They repaired the water supply system in the eastern part of Mostar, they linked it up, and then when the conflict broke out between the HVO and the ABiH in May 1993, the HVO turned the water off again.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That really is true. I'm sorry about it, but it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But why would they first repair the water supply system and then turn it off?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already said that I would leave that to historians. It's for them to look into the matter, but it's very easy to establish why this was done. It's the best form of punishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: One more question about this. That is a conclusion that you have drawn on the basis of the information you had at the time, information that you concluded that the HVO turned the water off deliberately. They didn't want it to go to the eastern side.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, how else should I have understood this? All of a sudden I no longer had water or electricity. It wasn't possible to leave one part of the town. This is the worst kind of camp one could have. It was the worst kind of camp in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well, but this is not something that you saw with your own eyes. You have no direct information that the HVO authorities ordered someone to turn the water off. You don't know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that the valves were located in positions where this could have been done. They weren't on the left bank. The left bank didn't turn off its water supply system. In that case, someone else did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I agree, someone else did that.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That other entity is on the other side; it's the HVO. The armija, the ABiH wasn't in a position to turn off the water for the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pejanovic, please listen to the question. I'm not trying to persuade you that the army did this, all I'm asking you is the following: Everything you've said is fine, but do you have any direct knowledge according to which the HVO issued an order for the water supply system to be turned off?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That's what I'm asking you about. So it is your assumption when you say that the HVO wanted the water supply system to be turned off.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can take it in that way if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. A few other details that I nevertheless think are important. With regard to Exhibit 09517, you indicated two water supply points. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Later we had a look at the map. Tell me, those two -- those two hydrants, in the immediate vicinity of the demarcation line --

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they're very close to that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That's really a war zone.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I've understood you correctly, if I understood you correctly, you do not claim that your vehicles and your staff were deliberately targeted.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is what I said yesterday. I'll repeat it. After a certain period of time, I can't how much time had passed, they started firing at that location where we would get water from, and then the water supply ceased at that point and we then went to the yard of the electrical utility group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But at the time when you still went to the court area, there was still fighting?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not really. To be quite true -- to be quite frank, there were periods of calm. I don't know what they were re-organising, restructuring; I don't know. But there were periods of calm, and one almost had the impression that peace had been re-established.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: One more question about the water. I wouldn't want this to be wrongly interpreted later on. On page 79, line 19 of the transcript, you said with regard to the quality of the water that the water was the colour of blood.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You didn't want to say that there was blood in the water.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said that chlorine had been put into the water to destroy the bacteria, and as a result, the water was a reddish colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: A little later, on page 83 of the transcript, you mentioned -- you mentioned a flood in the Neretva which was the result of a valve.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Since you're an old inhabitant of that area, could you tell the Court how far upstream that dam is?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was about two and a half kilometres or three kilometres from the point that we had -- from the point where we tanked water.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That entire part up to the dam was under HVO control?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not correct. The right part was but not the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, but right up to the town?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, up to the time, because of the 30th of June, 1993, the army took the positions in the northern camp and right up to the Salakovac tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That's correct, but who had access to the dam?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At that time.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about any actions of sabotage with regard to that dam?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only when this event happened, because the army was on part of the M17 street and behind the M17 street and between the textile industry complex, so the army was really not in a position, not even theoretically speaking, to have positions around the dam.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you have any more direct and detailed knowledge with regard to how this was blown up, with regard to who issued the order to carry out this act?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no such information. It was said that a torpedo was used, which seems more logical to me. I doubt other forms of explosives were used. As I have already said, I've spent 24 months in the -- in the marines. I was a mine specialist and a diver, but I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So this is not something that you can claim, is that what you're saying? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I have one more question. According to the information I have, in that area where the dam was, the armija, the ABiH, had the left bank, held the left bank near the dam and the entire area. So it was possible for the armija to gain access to the dam on one side, and the HVO had access to it on the other.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the shut-off valve on one of the sites had been blown up but I can claim that the army didn't even approach -- didn't get as close as a hundred metres from the dam, but it did have the left bank under its control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But you weren't there at the time. You don't have direct information.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct but I did pass by a few times. I went over the hill. I would descend from the firing range and would go to Zutina and then continue through Vratica up north.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's go back to Mostar. You mentioned a number of shelling incidents, sniper incidents. At one point in time you started discussing something and then you were interrupted. In the course of conflict between the ABiH and the HVO from May, 1993, onwards, could one say that the Serbian forces or, rather, the JNA shelled both the left and the right part of Mostar, both the eastern and western part of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me try to explain this a little more precisely. It's correct that the Serbs did sometimes shell the eastern part of the town, but as soon as there were -- as there was fighting in the part of Bosnia from Foca, Kalinovik, and further on towards Bihac, well, this is the way in which they would fight the war. But they would relieve one part of the battlefield in order to relocate forces to another part. So when this happened in part of Bosnia, then there would be shells falling on the left bank of Mostar. This didn't last for very long, but you never knew for how long -- how long this would last. When one shell falls, you wait for the next one to fall. So such things did occur. But on two or three times the Serbs also neutralised a PAM, an anti-aircraft machine-gun on the Hum. Or, rather, they would silence it and then in the afternoon hours the fire would again be opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. I haven't finished my question yet. Speaking as a layman, does this mean - please confirm this or reject it - from May, 1993, and onwards, in Mostar there were shells fired by the ABiH, there were shells fired by the HVO, and there were shells fired by the armija. Was there anyone else or were those the participants?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Serbian shells didn't fall that frequently, but it's lucky for the eastern part of the town that the Serbs were the least active. They didn't shell that much. That's -- that was very fortunate for us. Otherwise, we would have been attacked from two sides. There was no way out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You said that the shells -- the Serbs shelled the least but they did shell occasionally.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You said why you thought that this was the case. You said that the Serbian forces or the JNA forces also shelled HVO positions on Hum hill.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. But they were no longer the JNA forces at the time. They were really Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. So these were local forces.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I make a clear distinction here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But did you have any information on how far away from Hum the Serbian forces were, the ones that could shell the town?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Serbian positions were the town exits above Blagaj, at the town limits. Let's say the last line was near the Herceg Stjepan location. There were bunkers there. And there was also a plateau which you arrive at when you head from Gorojnica [phoen] to Blagaj. I can't remember the name. And there were Serbian positions at Cobanovo Polje too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What sort of artillery weapons did the Serbs use when they opened fire?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know - and why I know is a different story - but on two or three occasions they used a Maljutka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. I was interested in Maljutka. Do you know what the range of a Maljutka is?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't, because Serbs were on the eastern part of the front, above Mostar, and in the direction of Hum hill. Don't just focus on one location. I don't know where artillery fire was opened from, but that is a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I won't go back to the tragic death of your colleague Jugo who was killed in front of your warehouse, in front of your station opposite the department store. A lot of questions were put to you about that. But just one other matter. As far as you can remember - and yesterday you started talking about this - you said that this happened after the peace agreements that were concluded.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in any event, it was shortly after a cease -- shortly after a truce had been signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Referring to the Washington Agreement, are we?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Washington Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let's not go back to the subject of the film. We had a look at that 360-degrees photograph. P9139 was the number. It was on the screen for a long time, and at one point I saw that from the street that your station is located in and right behind the traffic sign, I saw in the distance in western Mostar the Hotel Bristol. Did you notice that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite possible. Yes, it's possible that Hotel Bristol could be seen, because that building is higher than the other buildings. If you just move a step to the left from the pavement, yes, you'll see it for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that that was one of the possible positions from which the sniper shot?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I laughed a little ironically, and I apologise for that. I really do. I don't think they would shoot at their own people, for heaven's sake.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I didn't say who, I'm just saying --

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was the BiH army that was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, I apologise. It wasn't my intention --

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't mine either. I apologise to you, too, for that ironic laugh. But the BH army was there. I don't suppose it attacked its own people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I really do apologise. I just noticed that that might be the building and my colleagues told me that that was in indeed the Bristol Hotel. I thought it was the bank building. I didn't know that the Bristol Hotel was on this side of the Bulevar, so yes, that's right, that's right, that's quite right.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that, I thought it was across, opposite, because it looks far in the distance on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You were asked yesterday about distances and your assessment of distances with respect to two particular events. You didn't want to go into the details, of course, because it's difficult to assess distance, but I'm going to read out to you some figures that I read from the map. From the Razvitak building to the bank building called the Glas bank building, the distance by road across Tito's bridge is 500 metres. Would that roughly correspond to the distance?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't doubt it because I made a free assessment and I said that -- I told you the distance roughly speaking. It wasn't my intention to make the distance greater or smaller. I reacted quite spontaneously by giving you a rough estimate, but I absolutely do believe what you checked out and what you've just told us. I have no reason to doubt it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, the second distance, from the position of Stotina to the Saric Harem cemetery, that's the second incident we talk about, if you take the road across the nearest bridge, it would be about 70 -- 700 metres.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think 700 metres. I think that is my assessment too. That would be the distance. It depends where you were standing at Saric Harem, because Saric Harem is a rather long cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: From the south side.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. I said we were somewhere in the middle of Saric Harem cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In your assessment - you know the area - if we say that it was the middle of the Harem, the middle of the cemetery?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as the crow flies, this could be a little different, but for the weapons that can be used from that distance, it's just a negligible distance. So whether it's 700 metres or 800 metres, it doesn't matter, especially if you have optic sights on your rifle. Then I think it's quite irrelevant whether it's 700 metres or 800 metres. It's not one or two kilometres, it's just a hundred metres here or there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you think it's irrelevant that we -- and we can say that we have at least 500 metres in both cases, that any sniper can hit that target.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I say, we were somewhere halfway along the cemetery, the Harem. So there can only be a slight difference if we -- you measured it from Hasan Brkic bridge to the beginning of the Harem, there can only be a difference between 50 to 100 metres, not more than that. That can be the discrepancy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But my question is how far does that accuracy, the accuracy of a sniper?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think 50 metres is irrelevant. A hundred metres is irrelevant. Because you have, for example, the M48 rifle that could hit its target at two kilometres. And if you had optic sights, you could target anyone at that distance. At least, that's what I learnt when I did my military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, let's not you and I enter into that discussion now. We're losing time. But when I say 100 metres here or there, I referred to the projectile, and we agree there. But the possibility of hitting a target, that is to say a man targeting with this weapon, 100 metres at a distance of 500 metres is a lot. It's 25 per cent -- or 20 per cent. A fifth, shall we say. All right, you're not an expert in ballistics, that's what you said, so you don't know how much that can influence accuracy.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on yesterday's transcript, page 126, you once again had to draw on the map, and you placed a J on the map, the letter J, for that last incident near the court building, I think it was. That's what I jotted down here in my notes. And that was right up at the battlefield line, the separation line at Santiceva. Right up at the front line.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm trying to find my way here. Well, I can't seem to find my way on the map today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Never mind, we'll get to that later on. You wrote in a J.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it, thank you very much. I do apologise, I really do. I found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How much time do you need? How many more minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, to be quite frank, I have two or three brief questions but I'd like to check through my notes because I took quite a bit from my learned colleague Mr. Karnavas and some from my friend Nozica. I would need five to ten minutes, maximum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm giving you five minutes and then I'll just cut off the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pejanovic, we heard something this morning towards the end of your testimony, and a little yesterday as well, about certain positions of the BH army in eastern Mostar. Now, in eastern Mostar, you also had the positions of the command of the BH army and also the positions of the artillery; right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command, yes, but the artillery no, because the BH army did not have any artillery in that area. Mortars, yes; guns, cannons, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And the artillery?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just mortars, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I see. Right. Fine. Now, what about the mortar positions? Were they distributed along certain targets that were targeted multiple times?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can only talk about two positions that I know about. One position was towards the Serbs and the other position was probably facing the western part or the HVO, if I can put it that way. As to other positions, I really don't know, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And did these positions -- well, they were mobile units, weren't they, and they changed their positions frequently, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were mobile units but I can't say because I'm not an expert so I don't want to venture an answer about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: On page 42 of yesterday's transcript, line 1, you said that the police station in eastern Mostar was hit by artillery from Hum hill.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And that was a military target, was it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a police building, a police premises, and the police still not had been divided up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And it wasn't part of the army?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because that was in the morning of the 9th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see, the 9th.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the 9th. Or, rather, it might have been towards noon but it was on the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mentioned yesterday another incident with the Territorial Defence or, rather, the people who stopped you, and you said that it was the Territorial Defence judging by the insignia.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It said so on their sleeves, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now, we had the HVO, we had the BH army, yesterday you told us of the existence of the Territorial Defence, but later on during the day you mentioned the HOS, the HOS at one point.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just add the Territorial Defence was there from the time when the HVO had completely become organised and taken over the battalion. Then HOS was there, and how many HOS forces there were, what their strength was I really can't say. I don't want to delve into matters of that kind. But I do know that when Kraljevic was killed we went to put out a fire towards Siroki Brijeg and to put out a fire in the forest, in the park, and that the members of the HVO didn't allow us to enter into the Bishop's house hall area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, I wanted to ask you something about that, but to save time first of all tell me, please, to the best of your recollections, in a word, when was that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could have been --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I mean the integration, I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it must have been after the 30th of June, 1992, when the HVO officially took over.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it officially took over civilian authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Mr. Kraljevic. I think he was a colonel, had the rank of colonel there at that time, or perhaps general, and he received a decoration from the president of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say Alija Izetbegovic. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. Well, please believe me. I just mentioned him just by chance in this context. He was not somebody who was interesting as far as I was concerned because he was somebody who appeared at one point and then disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, with respect to HOS again, that existed and then disappeared. Do you know that HOS had more Muslim members than Croat members?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only do I know that there were more Bosniaks than Croats, but unfortunately that there were Serbs as well as members of HOS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So it was a multinational multi-ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether you can refer to it like that but I say that there were Serbs there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right, fine, very well. Was it then a predominantly Croatian military organisation?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that it had the Croatian components as being in the majority but I also say that there were Serbs within its formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you. I would have couple of questions, but since we are squeezed, I would give up. [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Pejanovic, very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I suppose you had agreed so as to have the questions put by the three counsel who put them, is that so? So no re-direct examination by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Mindua wanted to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could the witness briefly clarify on one general issue I did not understand when he testified yesterday. The witness stated that on the 9th of May, 1993, a conflict broke out in Mostar between the Croats and the Muslims and that the firefighters in Mostar had been ordered to hand in their equipment to the unit headed by Josip Skutor. When you say conflict between Muslims and Croats, what do you mean? Because we are in the Mostar municipality. On that date, on the 9th of May, 1993, were there two armies or armed groups? Was there a Croat armed group and another Muslim armed group, or was it only members of an ethnic group starting to look for members of another ethnic group, be they civilians or military to assault them? Did you understand the question? Can you answer it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to say, unfortunately, that this was no kind of ethnic conflict or a conflict between groups. It became a very significant war that flared up and lasted for almost a year; about eight or nine months, in fact. The fact is, and once again unfortunately, unfortunately for the town of Mostar and its citizens, that in 1992, as I said, this so-called Mostar Battalion was formed which was a precursor to the BH army and its members later on. And at that point in time, and I'm thinking of this Mostar Battalion, which became the BH army later on, its command and headquarters was partially put up in the Vranica building and a part of the forces were put up at the Mostar Hotel. At the beginning of the conflict in 1993, a group of citizens, as you know full well, I'm not going to tell you anything new, 13 of them disappeared from Vranica and their fate is not known to the present day. The other group that was in Hotel Mostar managed to cross the separation line and organise itself into, if I can say, a defence on the other side. Now, from that point in time, the BH army began to be created, established, and the MUP as a component part of that military formation was added onto the BH army, joined to the BH army, although the MUP in fact was functioning as an independent operative unit and did the kind of work that MUP was supposed to do to defend the internal order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. We shall have the opportunity to deal with such matter again. As to the admission of exhibits, yes, yes unless there is another question by the Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have two tiny questions that I would like to put. Yesterday you have said that your beautiful red fire engine was equipped both with a blinking blue light and with a signal siren horn. You said you did not use these because it was pointless. Why did you consider it pointless to use these elements?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, quite simply what use would it be using a siren or a blinking light in a street where there's nobody? Because there's shelling going on. What purpose would there be to use your siren or your blinking lights if you're moving through an empty town? You're not going to come across a single man out in the street until you reach your fire, because there was the general alarm that had been sounded and people were taking refuge in shelters. I also said yesterday that we had in light of day a curfew; that is to say, we weren't allowed to move around. And I will repeat: I'm very sorry that I didn't take my card, my permit that allowed me to move around 24 hours as a member of the fire brigade. So there were only us and the MUP members. We were the exceptions from this rule, from this curfew and ban of movement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe you even without seeing your permit. And the second question is: Was the HVO ever approached about the snipers? To your knowledge, has anyone ever brought to the knowledge of the HVO, of some authority, the fact that there was snipers shooting at the fire brigade and its -- its institutions and its personnel?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite frank, I think I said yesterday at one point that I was the last person who ought to have done that. I reported to the civilian protection staff and headquarters regularly, the casualties we came across, the property damaged, and so on, and the problems we encountered. Now, whether they, according to their chain of command, informed anybody and what way they did so if they did, I really can't say. I can't enter into their affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Karnavas -- yes, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise. Perhaps I did not understand the proposal of the conclusion correctly, but it seems to me that there was a difference between the English interpretation and what we heard in the B/C/S version. I'm not clear whether we're going to continue on Monday with this witness's testimony so that the three Defence teams who have prepared their cross-examination will go ahead. Now, if we're not going to have an opportunity of cross-examining the witness, then I would like to ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this morning and yesterday I said that the Defence counsel, all of them, were to agree among themselves in order to make sure that we would finish this hearing at quarter to two. This is what I stated yesterday. So you were supposed to just agree among yourselves. This is what I understood. When Mr. Karnavas took a long time putting his questions, then I gave the floor to Mr. Praljak and his counsel, so I did not know at all that you had failed to agree among yourselves. Now, if you wish to put very important questions, you have a few minutes to do so. I personally, I had questions, but let's not forget that the health of this witness is rather frail. I didn't want to harass him, but if you want to use your rights as Defence counsel and if you want to put questions to him, do it for a few minutes already. But they must be really essential.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, I will respect your decision and abide by it. I would just like us to decide on certain rules of procedure. On several occasions when we discussed this matter and how we are going to conduct cross-examination, that perhaps there would not be the possibility of all the Defence teams agreeing, and why should we agree when we might have different concepts for our cross-examination and different Defence cases? That's why I think we ought to decide on certain rules of procedure. My proposal would be as follows: We know how much time is allocated for the cross-examination and each Defence team should be given one-sixth of that time and they should adhere strictly to that one-sixth. Once -- if they have agreement from another Defence counsel, then they can have more time or less time, depending on the agreement among Defence counsel, and that is how we shall be able to avoid similar situations. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall discuss this on the Bench, but one thing was clear for me and my fellow Judges: You were to agree among yourselves as to the use of your time. Now, if there is no agreement -- well, you suggest one-sixth as a rule. Why not? But we do not want harm you and your client. If you do have any questions, just put them now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since it doesn't involve only myself but also my colleagues, Mr. Jonjic and Mr. Ibrisimovic, if you give me permission to put questions, then they should be allowed as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Pejanovic. I'm Vesna Alaburic, attorney from Zagreb. I'm representing General Petkovic. In compliance with the ruling of the Court, I shall reduce my questions to the minimum. And what I would like to clarify has to do with circumstances, dangerous circumstances, that your people and your vehicles were exposed to when carrying out very dangerous tasks. Yesterday, on page 56 of the transcript, I think that there was a mistake, because it says that out of your entire personnel, 14 were killed -- 14 were wounded and 15 were killed.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's a mistake. Not 15 but 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Shall we agree, then, that some of your colleagues were killed when putting out fires and some were killed simply as residents of East Mostar who found themselves in some dangerous situations, exposed to fire?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was perhaps one case of such nature. Everybody else was killed on duty. Whether they were going to work or going back home from work, it's the same as working. And in one occasion the person had a serious health problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you. But I would like to know this: Those who were wounded or who were killed when putting out fires, let me put questions to you in relation to that. Based on the information on the members who were casualties, you said that Edo Dostovic was wounded.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Alija Jakupovic twice?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Emir Vilic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mirzo Bratic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And Elvir Demic.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Based on your information, Mirzo Bratic was also wounded once but that was unrelated to the putting out of the fire.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was injured once when working. A shell hit a building where we were putting out fire, and a piece of concrete crumbled off and hit him on the head, and he didn't have a helmet on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: These five cases, we agreed that these people were wounded when putting out fires. In addition to them, are there any other of your colleagues who were wounded or killed when putting out fire?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody was killed, but people were wounded, yes. I usually say "fortunately." Fortunately, these were injuries without serious consequences. People were grazed by bullets and so on. There was superficial wounds. We also have one case that wasn't described, that of Miodrag Kandic, who, when putting fire in 1992 was hit by a shrapnel in his arm, and that simply wouldn't heal, that wound, because a piece of material from his jacket was lodged in the wound. So there were cases like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You said so, and you wrote in your book, that you had a vehicle, a truck, TAM 125, and then you had another Zastava 650.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And then you had a Lada Niva.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: As far as I could understand, you had these vehicles throughout the time.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mostly, but occasionally these vehicles were not operational.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: They were not operational, if I understood you well, mostly because of minor things such as tyres, flat tyres and so on. But none of the vehicles were put out of order due to intense artillery fire.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said so. There was an artillery shell that hit our vehicle. It hit it accidentally. It was a mortar shell, and it wasn't done on purpose.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. We heard that, that it hit the cab of the vehicle. Was the vehicle completely unusable?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't usable for a long time after that. It was damaged quite severely. And we had to invest quite a lot into repairing that vehicle, and then after that we lost it again.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, let us deal with the damage on the vehicles and how your people were wounded. Can you link this information with your statements as to how you were daily exposed to the firing of snipers, mortar fire, and so on. This is on page 51 of your book. You were also exposed to artillery fire as well as the fire of an anti-air machine-gun. Based on the information about the damage sustained by your vehicles and injuries of your people, one could conclude that those who fired on your fire brigade unit were either not -- were not skilful when targeting. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't say so. I think that these people were quite skilled and trained in artillery warfare. I think that what happened was a result of just chance, or that's how chance would have it. Sometimes you survive a very dangerous situation by chance. So I think it's all due to chance, not to lack of skill. I didn't add anything to what I wrote in my book.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. That's right. It seems that you do not doubt the skill and the competence of people using artillery weapons, and since your vehicles were mostly operational --

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not the whole time. There were periods when they were not operational for a number of days on end. And sometimes we would be left with just one or perhaps two vehicles. It all depended on the current situation and how much damage was inflicted. Let me give you a better example: For example, your battery is out and you have no way of getting another one, and that could happen even without any fire hitting your battery. So if your vehicle is all right but the battery doesn't work, you can't use the vehicle. And all of this was due to that unfortunate war. And despite the best of will, you still couldn't be mobile because of things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We could agree that the HVO was relatively well equipped with artillery weapons, and they were also relatively well equipped for targeting targets that they wanted to hit. So could we then agree that they didn't have as their objective to put out of order fire-fighting trucks since you had at least one operational?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to give you a very basic, decent answer. The area is so small that it doesn't matter whether it will hit you directly or not. However, if a shell lands in your immediate vicinity, you become a victim nevertheless. In our vicinity there was the war hospital where all the wounded, all the injured were treated. I'm not going to say that this was done on purpose, but frequently this facility was targeted. I don't know whether they targeted specifically or not, but it was hit, and since we were so close to the war hospital, that affected us as well. Let me give you another fact never mentioned so far: In the department store Razvitak, in the basement there was a public kitchen, and everybody knew well that people came there when the food was distributed, and they came there at different times, sometimes at 10.00 in the morning sometimes at 5.00 in the afternoon, and it was enough to have one of those unfortunate shells fired at that location and you would be a victim. Maybe they didn't target you specifically, but you would still be injured.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This department store Razvitak, was it destroyed?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I don't mean whether it was destroyed, targeted.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Its main beam was destroyed, and as a result of that, the 64 flats which were built on top of that, were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And the public kitchen remained operational?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that area, yes, because this is on the south-east part of that building, and people had to work there under very, very difficult conditions because there was no other place where they could have put up a public kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pejanovic, in view of the circumstances, I will put just a few more questions to you, depending on your answers. When you were putting out fire on the front line on the first defence line, you, when describing that, wrote in your book that when you came to put out fires, the firing at the building continued. You also described how you arrived at the first front line based on which I conclude that you came to put out fires in facilities. Even while the combat operations were on, you went, despite of that, to the front line.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You concluded quite accurately that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us from the point of view of your colleagues and the ability to carry out your job, wouldn't it not have been more rational to wait for the fighting to conclude and then to start putting out fires?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My dear lady, please understand this: When we went out to these facilities to put out fire, the members of the BH MUP were precisely there. And if we let those buildings burn down, there would have been no more defence. We had to do that, and for a while we did that successfully.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have one additional question about the Razvitak department store. Can you tell us who destroyed that facility, the department store and the flats above it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is how it was: The flats were burnt in 1992, but the main construction frame remained intact. It wasn't destroyed. At one point when they shelled, the main, the central beam or pillar was hit and from then on the facility wasn't safe any more, wasn't usable. Later on, when the facility was demolished, now they completely demolished the residential area, leaving only the commercial premises of the building.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you speak of 1992 and how the building was damaged then, you mean the JNA and the forces of Bosnian Serbs; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it came from that direction. If you are facing the building, it had some flats on the eastern side and some on the western side. If you want me to be more detailed about it, I would be more likely to agree with you that the flats that were set on fire on the eastern side, that Serbs were to be blamed for that. And as for the ones that were burnt on the western side, that the fire came from that direction, from the west.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you for allowing me this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The clock is ticking.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I fully understand that we are being run over by time, but with your leave, I will put two or three questions even though I planned to put much more.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I really need to go out. I need to go to the bathroom. I cannot stay here any longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall make a ten-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We've got ten minutes left on the tape, so, Mr. Jonjic, you have five minutes, and the next Defence counsel will also have five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pejanovic, I only have two or three questions for you on behalf of Mr. Valentin Coric. If you answer briefly, we'll be able to deal with them in five minutes. Your fire-fighting unit was part of the civilian protection; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: At the time of an imminent threat of war or at a time of war, what is the legal position of the civilian protection with regard to the authorities?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite frank, you're the first person who has put such a question to me. The relation was not quite defined and it was ugly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Let's not go into lengthy explanations since we don't have much time. As far as the level of your responsibility or discipline is concerned with regard to the government, executive authority, with those in power at the time, was your level of responsibility higher or lower than in peacetime?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should have been higher.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You know that in the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina general mobilisation had been declared at the time?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Did this general mobilisation give the authorities, the municipal authorities, the right to issue you orders according to which you should restructure the fire-fighting organisation?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that they had such authority but such things were never implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yesterday, you were saying that the decision dated the 22nd of January, 1993, signed by Jadran Topic, was a decision you didn't want to implement and a decision that you didn't implement. In the course of the cross-examination today, you were presented with a number of prior decisions from 1992 in which you were also ordered to restructure the organisation. You didn't act on any of those decisions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me to clarify something: I said that with regard to the decision dated the 17th of December, well, we didn't receive it, but as far as the other decision dated the 22nd of January is concerned, we didn't implement it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: That's clear. Yesterday you didn't provide us with information on your educational background. Naturally the Chamber has the power to compel the witness to answer such questions. I won't go into these details, however. All I will do is ask you in order to be a commander is it necessary to have a certain level of qualifications and did you have such qualifications?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, you only needed fools to go to war, fools who would comply with orders. I have answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: My question is specific: In order to be a commander, and you were a commander for quite a number of years, in order to be a commander, was it necessary to have the relevant qualifications?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I did meet the criteria.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what sort of educational level you need?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I qualified as a plumber.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. After not having implemented the decision that you received from Jadranko Topic, or signed by Jadranko Topic, you said that the only form of punishment you were submitted to was that you weren't provided with food in the northern camp.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I wasn't provided with logistics either, not just food.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: The northern camp was called the Tihomir Misic barracks for a certain period of time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, that's not correct. I'm not quite sure, perhaps it was. Don't hold this against me, I really don't know, but I know that at the time of the JNA it was called the Mostar Battalion barracks, today it's the Hujdur Hujka barracks, but I don't know what it was called at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Was she in Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, she was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Tell me whether Siroki Brijeg is a municipality which is mainly inhabited by Croats.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I would also like to point out that my wife is a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Regardless of the fact that you were the commander of a fire-fighting unit which was at the disposal of the ABiH, can you tell me whether your daughter had any unpleasant experiences in Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Luckily, that was just a stopover. She spent time with her uncle in Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: But did she have any unpleasant experiences?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you said on page 47 that in the area controlled by the ABiH, 600 Serbs remained and 246 Croats.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's information I obtained when we were distributing humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many Muslims remained in the territory of Mostar in the area under the control of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. All I know is that a lot of them went to other countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: How many remained there?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, not far from the headquarters of your fire-fighting association you said there was a hospital, that there was the war hospital.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Do you know when this -- when they started building the war hospital or, rather, do you know when the war hospital became functional, not when it was actually built?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was at the beginning of the conflict, or perhaps a little earlier, but I think that it was after the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: I only have another two brief questions. When Mr. Jugo was killed, your colleague and friend, was anyone else present?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Dzemo Barakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And one more question: Now that the conflict is over, do you participate in the power structure? Do you have a political function?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: After the war, did you have any political function?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Which function?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the president and vice-president of the town hall and I was an assemblyman on three occasions. On one occasion it was for the party for Bosnia and Herzegovina. I didn't really belong to any party and I don't belong to any party today, but this is another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Were you a candidate for the Party for Democratic Action?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was never a candidate for that party or for the party for Bosnia-Herzegovina, but we were taken through that party for marketing reasons in order to receive a mandate in the council.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I only have one question for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The fire brigade unit must have some sort of a duty book.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Are all the incidents when you intervene recorded in it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Does it also record interventions during the period we have been discussing, interventions when fires weren't the result of the wartime action?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regardless of the cause of the fire, it was necessary to register the fires. Sometimes we would -- we would always register in this book.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have such a book?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We did have such a register.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence counsels, I'd like to thank the Defence counsel who have just put these last questions. Witness, your testimony is now finished. I thank you for having testified here for eight hours. You've answered a number of questions, and I hope you are not too tired as a result of it. I wish you a safe trip home, and I shall ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom. In the meantime, I will ask Mr. Karnavas to let us know which exhibits he would like to tender into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It's 1D00389, 388, 390, 392.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The exhibits mentioned by Mr. Karnavas [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] 1D00388, 1D00390, and 1D00392.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Before adjourning this hearing, we have admitted the exhibits of the Prosecution this morning, but we have to mention that these are tendered under seal. Given that names are mentioned in these documents, we need to specify that these are tendered under seal. I would like to thank all the people who have taken part in this hearing, and we shall meet again for our next hearing on Monday. We shall hear Mr. Donia. I hope he will be there. And we shall resume this hearing on Monday at 2.00, and I wish you a good weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 8th day of May, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.
